So `still`, the second shape: `on`, `off`, and `is`. It is
`reaching` with the specifics taken out -- there it was answered
calls cancelling missed ones, here it is any kind cancelling any
other -- and that is the argument for having built the general
mechanism rather than the one check. The first customer was about
people and the second is about a helmet, and neither needed a word
added to the grammar.

#### A space broke it, and no test had one

The first rule written against real data failed at once:

	"helmet" is not a blank a pattern fills in

A pattern source is one string split on spaces, and the device is
called **bike helmet**. `is=bike helmet` became two fields, the
second of which was not a blank at all.

Every test of the mechanism had passed. Every one of them had used
a value with no space in it -- `tries=2`, `among=amma` -- because
the examples were written by the person who had just written the
parser and was thinking in the shape of it. The blanks are
percent-encoded now, and `Describe` decodes them again, because the
escaping exists to survive a string and has no business in a
sentence a person reads: nobody should be told their rule did not
run because of `bike+helmet`.

The lesson is not "escape your strings". It is that **the examples
in a test are chosen by the same mind that chose the format**, and
the first real value broke what twelve tests had agreed on. Rules
written against this person's own data are worth more as tests than
anything invented.

#### Three rules, from his own senders

Two of the three things he picked were already expressible; the
third is what produced the pattern above. All three use kinds no
rule had touched -- places, bluetooth, calls made and received --
of which there were four entirely unused.

	still out when you would normally be home
	  every 30m, usually.home.arrives older than 90m, 19:00-23:00
	the helmet is still on
	  place.entered is home, then 15m, still on/off/is
	slept and woke  (extended)
	  the calls missed while they slept, folded into the greeting

The third was asked for as a rule of its own and built as an
extension instead. Two rules firing on the same unlock is two
announcements seconds apart, and the engine deduplicates within a
rule and not across them. One greeting that mentions both is what a
person would say.

### A filter for a browse, silently emptying a search

Owner, from his own transcript: *"yesterday I asked do you know Demi
Lovato. It said about Demi Lovato. But I literally hear Demi Lovato
in Spotify. It should have said to me."*

The first diagnosis was wrong and worth keeping for that reason.
The persona rule about looking everywhere is scoped to *"a person, a
place or anything of theirs"* -- things it could not know anyway --
and a singer is something it can answer from training, so the
explanation looked obvious: it never thought to check. Lines were
added to the persona saying that knowing the answer is not a reason
to skip the lookup, and three tries in a row then mentioned the
song. It read like a fix.

Then he sent the trace:

	Called event_recent
	  {"contains": "Demi Lovato", "days": 90}
	event_recent ok · 18ms
	  Nothing mentioning Demi Lovato was reported in the past 90 days.
	  The kinds that do exist ... music.state (199) ...

**It did look.** It reached for the right tool with the right
arguments and was told she had never been mentioned, in a sentence
that went on to list the very kind that mentioned her. The row was
in the table while the sentence was being written -- *Cool for the
Summer*, from his liked songs, the previous afternoon.

`q.Omit = event.Churn` -- `location.fix`, `music.state`,
`music.playing`, `music.paused` -- with an exception only when the
caller names one of those **kinds**. A `contains` search carries no
kind, so the exception never applied: **the one kind that holds
artists and tracks was excluded from every search for an artist or
a track.**

It is the same shape as the bare "call" answered with "nothing of
kind call today" above a list containing `call.received (13)`, which
is recorded a few sections above this one. A filter written to keep
a *browse* readable, applied to a *search*, where it does not narrow
the answer but empties it.

So a text search omits nothing now. The first attempt still held
back the position readings, on the reasoning that nothing in a
conversation wants a coordinate. Owner: *"a search should fetch
whatever is in the record, even the tiniest one."* He is right, and
it was the same mistake in a smaller size: a fix holds only a
latitude and longitude **today**, and what goes in a payload is the
sender's business. A phone that starts putting a street on its fixes
would be found by nobody, and nothing would say so.

#### Two lessons, and the second is the uncomfortable one

**Naming a thing is asking for it**, as much as naming a kind. Every
narrowing in this file should be asked which it is doing: making a
broad answer readable, or deciding what a specific question is
allowed to find.

And: **the fix that worked was not the fix for the bug.** Three
runs out of three mentioned the song after the persona change,
which is exactly what a correct fix looks like from outside. It
worked because the model sometimes asks by kind instead, and that
path was never broken. Had the owner not sent the trace, a prompt
change would have been credited with repairing a bug it never
touched -- and the bug would have gone on silently emptying every
other search. *A green result is not evidence until you know which
path it took.*

The persona lines stay. They are about saying his fact first rather
than second, which is a real thing and separate from this.

#### A test that asserted the bug

`TestPositionReadingsAreNeverReturned` failed on the change, and was
right to: it asserted that `{"contains":"12.911"}` finds nothing.
That was the old decision written down, and it had been passing for
as long as the search had been broken.

What survived of it is the distinction that actually matters.
**Asking for a kind is asking to browse it**, and a browse of
coordinates is useless, so `kind: location.fix` still answers that
there is nothing. **Naming a text is asking whether the record holds
it**, and the record is allowed to answer. The test now asserts
both halves, which is a better test than either version of the
rule.

Worth saying plainly: the commit went in with that test failing,
because the suite was run in the same command as the commit and the
failure scrolled past above the word "green". The guard added this
morning -- `make check` compiling the evals -- exists for exactly
this and was not used. Run the suite, read it, then commit.

### One thing said eighteen times

Owner, on a four-second answer of nine words: *"it took 4 seconds,
why the delay."*

Nothing was stuck. No tool ran. The median turn sends **32,574
input tokens** and gets back thirteen, and four seconds is roughly
what reading that costs.

	system prompt           4,207 tokens
	18 tool specs          15,444
	  of which "saying"     3,636
	deferred catalogue        690
	fixed every turn      ~20,342          + ~11,000 history and memory

The `saying` argument is 808 bytes of rules and examples, and
`Narrated` staples it to every tool. The model read the same
paragraph eighteen times a turn -- **18% of the fixed prompt to say
one thing eighteen times.**

It could not simply be deleted, and `saidWhile`'s own comment says
why: the model ignored this as a rule stated beside the tools and
obeyed it only once the examples lived in the schema property,
*"where the model is already reading"*. So the examples were doing
the work and the rules were the part that could move. One example
with the address stays in the schema; the rest is said once in the
persona.

	                     before      after
	saying argument    3,636 tok   1,467 tok
	fixed every turn  20,342 tok  18,299 tok   -2,043  (-10%)
	narration           8 of 8      8 of 8

#### The measurement had to be written first

There was no eval for this. Nothing anywhere judged whether a tool
call arrived with a sentence or whether the sentence was any good --
so the saving could have been taken and the narration quietly lost,
exactly as the search was quietly emptied earlier the same day.

`TestWhatTheNarrationCosts` was written before the change and run
before and after. Both runs: eight of eight.

**And the test's own verdict was wrong once, which is worth more
than the result.** It flagged *"reading your diary for tomorrow"* as
poor for being under six words. The baseline had answered the same
question with *"reading your diary for tomorrow, sir"* -- six words.
Both are far under the twelve to twenty the instruction demands, so
the real finding is that **neither version obeys the word count**,
and a threshold invented while writing the test nearly reported that
as a regression caused by the change.

What can be claimed: the 2,043 tokens, because that is a
measurement of a prompt and not of a model. What cannot: any
behaviour difference, on eight samples run once.

Nor can the latency be attributed yet. "hi" came back in 2.8s
against 5.2s earlier, and `in_tokens` was unchanged at ~32,600 --
the conversation history had grown by as much as the fixed prompt
shrank. A clean reading needs a fresh conversation.

#### Still on the table

`event_recent` is 1,710 tokens on its own, more than twice the
median tool, and grew twice today. The persona is 4,333 tokens and
has never been weighed against what it buys. Tool deferral already
works -- 18 offered rather than 58, for a 690-token catalogue -- so
the remaining weight is the tools that are offered, not the ones
that are not.

### A timer is not a guarantee

Owner, with the microphone open and nothing happening: *"it is
indefinitely listening. In that case, in case of failure it should
recover itself."*

	assist_satellite = listening
	last pipeline event: ten minutes earlier

Two faults, both introduced the same evening, and the second is the
one worth keeping.

**The cap cannot cap itself.** `TURN_MAX` ends a turn that runs too
long and it is a timer, so anything that cancels it removes the only
thing that was going to end the turn. The wake-word interrupt added
hours earlier does precisely that: it abandons the open turn, which
forgets the cap, and the stale `RUN_END` that follows forgets it
again. The log shows the whole thing in three milliseconds at
16:59:05 -- wake word, `RUN_END`, idle sound -- and then nothing at
all while the microphone stayed open.

So the recovery is not another timer. A thread runs for the life of
the process and asks one question every five seconds: **has the
microphone been open longer than any turn is allowed to be?** Forty
five seconds, comfortably past the cap so an ordinary long turn is
still ended by its own words. Nothing can cancel it, because nothing
holds a handle to it.

The general form: **a timer that something else can cancel is not a
guarantee, it is a hope with a clock on it.** Where the requirement
is that a thing cannot stay stuck, the check has to be owned by
something that does not take part in the thing going wrong.

**And the Mic Gate entity disappeared**, which Home Assistant said
three times and nobody read:

	Referenced entities number.bedroom_laptop_lva_mic_gate
	are missing or not currently available

It was cached on the satellite object. Every other entity is cached
on `state`. The satellite is rebuilt whenever Home Assistant
reconnects and `state` is not -- so each reconnect found its own
attribute empty, built another Mic Gate, appended it with a new key
and shifted every entity registered after it, until Home Assistant
dropped it from its registry altogether. The profile could then not
set the gate, and said so to nobody. It is looked up among
`state.entities` by `object_id` now.

Worth adding to the restart habits: **restarting the satellite does
not clear a stale entity list.** The satellite logged "Found 12
entities in state" and Home Assistant still had the old set; the
entity came back only after reloading the ESPHome config entry.
That is the move whenever an entity goes missing after a change
here.

#### The watchdog failed, in the way it was written to prevent

It wedged again within the hour, and the watchdog did not fire. The
log is six milliseconds wide:

	17:40:09.122  wake word, so the open turn is abandoned
	17:40:09.128  RUN_END for the abandoned turn
	17:40:09.139  RUN_START for the turn that replaced it
	              ... nothing at all for fifty-six seconds

The new turn set `_listening_since`; the abandoned turn's `RUN_END`
arrived eleven milliseconds later and cleared it. **The watchdog
read a timestamp that the failure path resets**, saw a microphone
that was not open, and skipped -- for fifty-six seconds, while it
was open.

The lesson had been written in this file one commit earlier: *the
check has to be owned by something that does not take part in the
thing going wrong.* Then the check was given a field the thing
going wrong writes to. Writing a principle down is not the same as
holding it, and the gap between the two was under an hour.

It keeps its own mark now, in a local that nothing outside the loop
can reach. It watches rather than asks.

**And the cause was fixed as well**, which two attempts had stepped
around while adding guards on top of it. Home Assistant answers an
abandonment with a `RUN_END`, and it arrives *after* the replacement
turn has started -- eleven milliseconds, measured. Taken at face
value it ends the turn that replaced it. A `RUN_END` within a second
of an abandonment is now ignored, the same way `_stopped_at` covers
the race that outlives the function holding it.

Two layers, deliberately: the race is fixed, and the watchdog
catches it if that is wrong again.

**Confirmed working** by the owner, 9 October 2026, on the sequence
that caused it -- a wake word spoken into a turn that was already
listening. Turns cycle and end on their own.

Three claims of "fixed" were made today that were not: a persona
change that passed three of three while the real bug sat untouched,
and this one twice. **The pattern is claiming a fix from the absence
of a failure.** A watchdog that has not fired, a search that returns
an answer, a test that goes green -- none of them say which path was
taken. Say what was measured, and say what was not.

### A say, not a veto

Owner, after the turn model was repaired that morning: *"audit the
Deepgram transcribed words and audio time -- it's not detecting the
end immediately?"*

He was right, and the cause was the repair. Deepgram's own log
gives the audit for nothing: it reports how many seconds of audio
arrived beside what it made of them, and natural speech runs about
0.6 seconds a word.

	BEFORE                                AFTER
	11.0s   2w   5.50  "Thank you."       2.6s  4w  0.65  "What is the time?"
	10.0s   1w  10.00  "Hello?"           2.8s  4w  0.70  "What is the date?"
	 3.0s   1w   3.00  "Hello?"           3.7s  6w  0.62  "What do you know about me?"
	median sec/word 1.80                  median sec/word 0.70

Eleven seconds of audio for two words. The silence was being sent
to Deepgram because the turn had not ended.

`keep_going` had no limit. Every time the model said the sentence
was unfinished the whole silence budget came back, and the only
backstop was the forty-five second timeout. The verdicts show what
that bought:

	still talking p=0.0131 over 1.7s of audio
	still talking p=0.0126 over 2.4s
	... eight times ...
	finished      p=0.9673 over 8.0s

Seventy-two of a hundred and thirteen verdicts were "not finished",
at a confidence of 0.013 -- near-certain -- and it turned finished
only when the eight-second window it is handed had filled. That is
a fact about the window, not about the sentence.

**The model may now hold a turn open twice and no more.** Two covers
what it is for, somebody drawing breath mid-thought, and bounds what
it was doing.

#### What the cap did and did not do

It did not improve the model. The verdict mix barely moved -- 64%
"still talking" before, 57% after -- because a bound does not change
what something says, only how far it is obeyed. What changed is the
median trailing silence, 1.80 to 0.70 seconds a word, and 0.70 is
natural speaking rate: there is almost no dead air left to cut.

Worth keeping in view: this was a fix that made things worse. The
model had been timing out at eighty milliseconds for as long as it
had existed, so repairing it was the first time anything it said
had ever been acted on -- and it immediately started holding every
short answer open for eight seconds. **The first day a component is
believed is the day to measure what believing it costs.**

And the audit itself is the reusable part. `deepgram live: Xs of
audio arrived over Ys: <text>` against the word count gives
seconds-per-word, and anything far above 0.7 is silence somebody is
paying for. No instrumentation needed; the bridge has been printing
it all along.

### The same habit at three distances

Owner, after the description could not tell him he was up late:
*"recent should count more than old."*

Every habit in the description was worked out over four weeks flat,
so a day three weeks ago counted exactly as much as yesterday.
Somebody who starts coming home at eleven this week goes on being
described as arriving at nine, and stays described that way until
three old weeks have aged out. **The description was true of the
month and wrong about tonight**, which is the only part anybody is
actually asking about.

So a habit is now counted three times over three lengths of time --
all four weeks, the last seven days, and today -- and **only the
differences are said**:

	place.entered "home": usually around 9pm, today at midnight.
	place.entered "home": usually around 9pm, but around 11pm this week.

Three identical hours say nothing and are left out, which is what
keeps it from becoming a nag. A habit with no usual hour is skipped
entirely: somebody who does a thing at no particular time cannot do
it late, and saying so would be noise.

No new evidence is read. It is the same moments the rest of the
description is built from, counted again over shorter windows.

#### Two tests that passed while measuring nothing

Worth recording because both were mine and both looked fine.

The first used three days of baseline against five recent ones,
which makes "usually" and "this week" **the same hour** -- so the
function correctly produced nothing, and the test asserted only that
the output did not contradict it. It passed by being vacuous. Fixed
by giving it three weeks of September to drift away from.

The second asserted `strings.Contains(got, "this week")` -- which
the *header* contains. It would have passed with no habit line at
all. Both now assert the sentence itself.

The general form, and it is the third time today: **assert on the
thing you are measuring, not on something that happens to appear
near it.** A green test that cannot fail is worse than no test,
because it is counted as evidence.

And one assertion was simply wrong about the code: it expected
"today at 12am" where `oclock` renders **midnight**. The code was
right and read better than the test that doubted it.

### What is trending in their life

Owner, after the three windows: *"there must be daily data -- what's
different from yesterday -- and weekly, what's different from last
week. Same for this month, last month, this year, last year, for
every event type. I might be listening to a song now, same as
yesterday, same last week and now too, so that's what's trending in
my life."*

A grid rather than a comparison. Four lengths of time, each against
the one before it, over every kind and value:

	today      vs yesterday
	this week  vs last week
	this month vs last month
	this year  vs last year

Each reports only what moved -- arrived, stopped, doubled, halved --
and at most three per window, because three is what somebody holds
and the fourth is read past. A steady habit is not a trend and is
left out: the same amount of the same thing is the opposite of news.

	this week: music.state "Demi Lovato" is new (18);
	           music.state "Anirudh" has stopped (was 5).

The months are twenty-eight days and the year is fifty-two weeks, so
each window is a whole number of the one below. Calendar months of
unequal length would make February look like a decline.

#### A window with nothing behind it says nothing

The rule that matters, and the reason this is honest on a young
database: **a window is reported only where there is a whole one of
itself before it.** Nine days of history cannot say anything about a
month, and "new this month" would mean only that the server was
switched on this month -- which is the shape of mistake that makes a
description untrustworthy in the week it is first read.

So as of 10 October 2026, on 8.6 days of events:

	today        needs   2 days of history -> works now
	this week    needs  14 -> in 5 days
	this month   needs  56 -> in 47 days
	this year    needs 728 -> in 719 days

The whole grid is built and three quarters of it is silent. It
fills itself in; nothing has to be changed for the week to start
speaking next Wednesday. That is the right way round -- the
alternative is a description that says a great deal in its first
week and is wrong about all of it.

### He writes his own rules now

Owner, on what the engine was always for: *"the main purpose of the
rule engine is not for me to create rules. He should understand the
pattern and create his own rules, so that next time a server event
arrives the rule is triggered, then Jarvis is hit with a trigger and
answers to me."*

Both sides of that already worked and had for weeks. The engine
wakes him when something happens; the description tells him what is
ordinary and what has moved. What was missing was the middle:

	events -> description -> trends -> [ nothing ] -> rule -> trigger -> he speaks

All twenty-five rules existed because somebody asked for one out
loud. `rules.Writer` was reachable only through a tool the model
calls when the person says "remind me if". Nothing ever decided by
itself that a thing was worth being told about.

`internal/app/noticing` is that decision and nothing else. On the
hourly pass, straight after the description is rewritten -- reading
an hour-old description to decide what to watch for would be a pass
spent on yesterday -- he is shown what he knows and the rules he
already keeps, and either asks for one rule in a sentence or says
there is nothing. The sentence goes to the same writer the tools
use, which turns it into a rule or refuses it. **Nothing he asks for
skips the validation anybody else's rule goes through.**

#### Written to refuse

The failure mode of this idea is not a bad rule, it is four hundred
rules. A model asked hourly whether anything deserves a rule will
find something, every hour, for ever.

So the bar is in the instructions and the examples are of saying no.
A rule is worth having only where the pattern is in the evidence
with counts, has happened often enough to be a habit, has something
that can go wrong, would change what they do, and is not already
covered by a rule he keeps. Everything else is nothing.

And three guards outside the prompt, because a prompt is a hope:

**One a day, six hours apart**, counted from the rules themselves
rather than a counter, so a restart does not hand him a fresh
allowance. Checked *before* the model is asked, since a call made
and then discarded is the allowance leaking money.

**An unreadable answer writes nothing.** A missed rule costs one
unremarked pattern; a misread one runs for ever.

**And his rules are their own kind**, `noticed`, with why he wrote
it kept on the rule. A rule nobody asked for has to be able to say
what it is for, or the only thing to do with it is delete it --
and deleting one of his is a different act from deleting one of
theirs. One is changing your mind; the other is telling him he was
wrong.

#### A third model

Owner, in the same breath: *"for profiling and rule engine creation
we can use claude-sonnet-5-5."*

There were two models and the split was about latency: `model` for
answering, `fast_model` for the greeting, which has two seconds
before a fixed sentence is said instead. Both of these passes are
the opposite trade -- nobody is waiting, and what they produce is
read back for weeks. A description is believed; a rule keeps firing.

So `slow_model`, used by the description, the judge and the writer.
Empty falls back to `model`, which is what they all did before.

#### And taking one back

Writing a rule and being unable to retire it is the same hole as a
memory that can never become wrong -- the third place it has turned
up. So the pass does both, and takes one back before it writes
another: the rules he keeps are what he is shown when deciding
whether to write, so a dead one left standing is itself a reason to
write nothing.

The prompt for this one is written to **keep**, which is the mirror
of the other and for the opposite reason. There the risk was four
hundred rules; here it is tidying away the one that would have
mattered next week. **A rule that has never fired is usually a rule
for something rare, which is exactly what a standing rule is for**
-- the phone failing to charge is worth hearing about precisely
because it is unusual, and a month of silence is the rule working.

Three guards again, and the last one matters most:

**Only after a week.** Written Tuesday and retired Wednesday is not
a companion changing his mind, it is thrashing, and the thing it
watches may simply not have happened yet.

**Only his own.** Rules the person asked for are theirs to keep or
drop. He has no business tidying them away.

**And only an id he was actually shown.** A model naming a rule it
was not given has invented one, and acting on that would let an
unreadable answer delete somebody's reminder.

Cancelled rather than deleted, so that asked why he stopped saying
something, the answer is in the table.

#### What to expect

Nothing, for a while, and that is the design. He has nine days of
data and three quarters of the trending grid is still silent. A pass
today is reasoning from almost nothing, and the bar is set so that
reasoning from almost nothing produces nothing.

The first interesting pass is after the week window opens, five days
from now. If he has written anything before then, the bar is too
low.

### A memory can become wrong

Owner, on the last of the three: *"old facts should be able to
expire."*

Twenty memories, none of which could ever stop being true. A fact
kept in September was read into every turn in October with exactly
the same weight as one written this morning, and a later memory had
no way to say it had taken over.

It is the same hole as a rule that cannot be retired and a sentence
that outlived its occasion, **and it is the worst of the three**: a
retired rule left standing fires when it should not, a stale
sentence stays silent, and a wrong memory is read into every single
answer.

His own data showed it plainly. Four memories about music, two of
them naming a favourite song:

	09-30  Favorite song              Everybody Wants to Rule the World
	10-07  Fireflies as favorite song Fireflies by Owl City
	10-07  Humbug by Elfman           Likes the song Humbug
	10-09  Vianney                    Likes the artist Vianney

`memories.stale_at` and `stale_why`, set rather than deleted, the
same as a cancelled rule: asked why he no longer believes something,
the answer should be in the row rather than gone with it.

**The part that matters is the reading, not the column.** Three
queries feed a turn -- the standing tier, the keyword search and the
vector search -- and all three now exclude a superseded memory.
Nothing else does, so everything that lists or audits them still
sees the lot.

#### Written to leave things alone

The judging prompt is the opposite of the rule-writing one. There
the failure was four hundred rules; here it is throwing away
something the person asked to keep.

**A person is allowed to be more than one thing.** Most pairs that
look contradictory are simply two facts: somebody can like two
songs, know two people of the same name, and have two routines. So a
memory is superseded only where a later one says something that
cannot be true at the same time -- where they live, what something
is called, an explicit correction -- and preferences are named as
the case never to touch. Liking a new artist does not stop them
liking the old one.

The same three guards as the rules: only after a day, only one at a
time, and only an id he was actually shown -- a model naming a
memory it was not given has invented one, and acting on that would
throw away something they asked to keep.

#### The three are now one shape

	Job.Said      outlived the occasion     fixed, the battery alerts
	noticed rules outlived the pattern      retire, after a week
	memories      outlived the truth        supersede, after a day

Each was found separately, by the owner noticing something was
wrong, and each turned out to be the same missing idea: **a thing
kept so it is not repeated has to be able to stop being true.** That
is worth remembering as a question to ask of anything new that
remembers: what makes this expire?

### He can ring people, and asks first every time

Owner, 10 October 2026: *"we can set an alarm right -- likewise,
there should be an option to call a person -- for that it should have
the contacts list on my phone."* Asked whether every call should be
put to him first, or only one on a name that was merely close:
**"confirm always."**

#### The server does not get the address book

The ask contained its own answer -- *it should have the contacts
list* -- and that is the one part not built. What goes to the phone
is a **name**. The phone looks the name up in its own contacts and
dials.

Three reasons, in order of weight:

1. **It is the only safeguard there is.** A server that will dial
   digits it was handed can be made to ring anybody by one misheard
   sentence. One that can only pass a name can only reach somebody
   already in the phone.
2. **It is the same way round as everywhere else here.** *The owner
   names the place and the server stores the name*; the sender
   resolves its own names and the server holds no lookup table. An
   imported address book would be the first table of other people's
   telephone numbers on a machine with no use for them, and would
   need keeping in sync for ever.
3. **It would bury what he actually uses.** Five hundred contacts
   against the ten people he has really called.

And the server is not blind without it. Every call the phone reports
names who it was with, so it already knows the list worth matching a
misheard name against:

	Alekhya Chintada 16   Amma 13   Kliffy 6   Megatron 3
	Vel Kumara 2   Gunalan 2   Ramesh 2   Muthu Selvi 1 ...

That list is short enough to read out, costs nothing to keep in step,
and is exactly the set of people a mangled name is likely to be one
of.

**It is not a gate.** Somebody never called before may still be a
contact on the phone, so a name that matches nobody is still rung
once he has said yes -- it is only asked about differently. Nothing
in the tool ever concludes that a person does not exist, for the
usual reason: a name out of speech-to-text that came out wrong looks
exactly like a name that is not in the list.

#### Confirm always, and why the voice channel is open at all

Anything that cannot be undone is normally kept off the voice list,
because a misheard sentence is the whole authorisation. A call is
exactly that kind of thing -- and being able to say *"call Amma"* is
the entire feature, so the gate is moved rather than removed: the
first call never dials. It comes back with the name it would ring
and the question to put, and only a second call carrying
`confirmed` places anything.

A name that merely sounds close is stricter still: it is sent back
for confirmation even when `confirmed` was passed, since the thing
needing agreement is *which person*, and the model agreeing with
itself is not that. **Kliffy** has already arrived from Deepgram as
*Cliffy* and as *Clifford*.

A telephone number is refused outright at both ends -- in the tool,
with an answer that tells the model to ask whose number it is and
ring them by name, and again in `calling.Body`, which is the last
place before the wire.

#### Two tools, which is what makes the list real

`call_people` lists, `call_place` writes, both in domain `calling`.
That is not symmetry for its own sake: **a write is refused until its
own domain has been read in the same turn**, so the names in front of
the model when it chooses one are read from events rather than
remembered from a conversation an hour ago. The machinery already
existed; the call tools get it by being shaped like everything else.

#### Getting there is the errand queue's job

`errand.CallPlace`, a hand beside the two alarm ones, its own secret
path on the phone (`[homeassistant] call_url`), and `Phone.Ring`
checking that the answer really came from the phone -- a captive
portal's cheerful 200 would otherwise read as a call that was placed.

Two differences from an alarm, both deliberate:

- **It expires after two minutes.** Somebody who asked to ring his
  mother and whose phone was unreachable for ten wants to hear that
  it did not happen, not to have it dial while he is in a meeting.
- **A failure is spoken.** `Sender.Told` fired only for `alarm.set`;
  it now fires for a call too, and more loudly, because he has
  already been told it is ringing and has stopped thinking about it.

With no `call_url` configured the tools are not registered at all. A
model holding a `call_place` that cannot work will say it is ringing
somebody and then explain why it could not, which is two sentences
worse than not having it.

#### The phone half

A third Tasker profile on port 1821, matching the call path, reading
one line of body as a name, and answering `phone-call-ok` once it has
dialled. Not `jarvis-call`: the assistant's name is configuration and
was FRIDAY before it was Jarvis, and a word on the wire that has to
be changed on the phone when he renames the assistant is a trap. The
two alarm tokens predate that rule and are not the example to copy.

Built and working, 10 October 2026. A third profile on port 1821
matching `/c/<secret>`, answering `phone-call-ok`, running a task
called `Jarvis Call`. The task reads `%http_request_body` directly,
which is how `Jarvis Alarm` already does it.

Resolving a name against the contacts turned out to have exactly one
route in Tasker, and three that look right and are not. Worth writing
down because every one of them was tried:

	Call action         digits only -- given "Amma" it dialled 2662 (T9)
	Contact Via App     resolves a contact, but only WhatsApp/Telegram
	                    offer a call mimetype -- VoIP, not a phone call
	Run Shell           runs as untrusted_app; `content query` returns
	                    empty stdout, empty stderr and an OK result
	JavaScript          Tasker 6 has no Java bridge: `android` is
	                    undefined, so there is no ContentResolver

What works is a chain of **Java Function** actions, and the trick that
makes it short is putting the name in the **path** of the contacts
filter URI, which removes every `String[]` argument:

	cr   = CONTEXT.getContentResolver();
	uri  = Uri.parse( content://com.android.contacts/data/phones/filter/%http_request_body );
	cur  = cr.query( uri, null, null, null, null );
	%ok  = cur.moveToFirst();
	%idx = cur.getColumnIndex( data1 );
	%num = cur.getString( %idx );
	Call  Number %num, Auto Dial

Measured: `.../filter/Amma` returned `+91 97899 66545`. That filter
URI is the dialer's own search, across full name, first name and
nickname, so **the phone does the near-matching too** -- "Alekhya"
finds "Alekhya Chintada" without the server having to.

Tasker was granted `CALL_PHONE` and `READ_PHONE_NUMBERS` over adb.
Without them the Call action will not even open for editing. Both are
reversible with `pm revoke`.

**A name nobody matches dials nothing, and that falls out of the
shape rather than being checked for.** With no row, `getColumnIndex`
and `getString` fail, the task stops at that action, and the Call
never runs. Tested by posting a nonsense name: `phone-call-ok` came
back, the log shows the task exiting with an error at action 6, and
no call was placed. The reply is Tasker's Quick Response, which
answers before the task runs -- so as ever, a 200 proves the message
arrived and nothing more.

### Confirm always was a boolean he set himself

Owner's own trace, 10 October 2026. The first `call_place` of a
fresh conversation, nobody having been asked anything:

	raw="[call_place {"who": "Alekhya Chintada", "confirmed": true}]"

The rule was *confirm always*. What was built was an argument named
`confirmed`, and the thing being asked to confirm was the thing
filling it in. **A flag the model sets is not a confirmation**, and
the only reason that call did not go straight out was the unrelated
read-before-write refusal.

#### The token is the easy half

`call_place` with a name now dials nothing ever. It returns the
question to put and a six-byte word made by the server, and only a
second call carrying that word can ring anybody. That much is the
same idea as *an identifier comes from the listing, never made up*,
which the writes already rely on.

#### The half that actually matters

A token proves the question was **asked**. It cannot prove it was
**heard** -- and a model can ask for one and hand it back in the
same breath, which is the assistant agreeing with itself and exactly
the bug in a new costume.

So the server asks a different question: **has the person said
anything since?** `SaidSince` already existed, returns only what the
person themselves said, and the pending call records the moment it
was handed over. No message after that moment means nobody has
agreed to anything, whatever the arguments claim.

	asked at T       the question is handed to the model
	spoken at T+n    the model says it out loud
	answered at T+m  they reply -- this is the only evidence
	rung             only now

It fails closed. A fault reading the messages reads as *not
answered*: a question repeated is a nuisance, a stranger's phone
ringing is not.

Four other ways in are shut at the same time, each with a test: a
made-up word, a word with no question behind it, a word answered
about one person used to ring another -- it rings what it asked
about, never what the second call carries -- and the same word used
twice.

#### What it costs

Calling is now always two turns. That is what *confirm always* means
and there is no version of it that is one turn, because one turn is
precisely the case where nobody was asked.

The pending question lives in memory and dies with a restart, which
is the right way round: a question nobody can remember being asked
should be asked again. It lasts three minutes, so a "yes" to
something else at lunch cannot ring somebody asked about at
breakfast.

### Speaker and mute take no confirmation

Owner: *"can i command to put to speaker, mute myself, record it?"*

Recording is not possible and was not built. Android 6 closed the
call-recording API, Android 10 cut microphone access during a call,
and the accessibility workaround everyone moved to was banned from
Play in May 2022; only a pre-installed dialer can reach that audio.
Tasker has a Record Audio action which simply would not get the call.

The other two are built and **deliberately not confirmed**, which is
the opposite of the decision one section above. The reason is the
room rather than the risk: each is undone by saying the opposite, and
both are asked for while somebody else is on the line, where *"shall
I put that on speaker, sir?"* said out loud is worse than being
wrong. They are silent for the same reason -- anything said here is
said into that call, and the tool's own result tells the model so.

One errand kind and one profile, not four. The body is two words --
`speaker on`, `mic off` -- and the task is four actions each with one
`If` on `%http_request_body`. Tested: each word runs exactly one
action and the other three report `IfFail`.

**Muting is the microphone off**, which is the one place the words
and the switch run opposite. Inverted at the tool, so nothing
downstream has to remember it, and there is a test whose whole job is
that inversion.

Twenty seconds rather than the call's two minutes. A call put on
speaker after it has ended is nothing but confusing.

#### And asked for with the call

Owner: *"call_place should take args speaker and mute, by default
they both are false."* Which is right, and the trace that started
all of this was exactly that sentence -- *"call Alekhya and put it
on speakers"* -- met with two separate thoughts.

So `call_place` takes them, both false unless asked for, and they
ride through the confirmation: the wish is recorded on the pending
call and taken from either call, since *"and on speaker"* may come
with the name or with the yes.

**They go a few seconds behind the call**, not with it. The dialler
has to be up before the speaker means anything, and nothing here is
told when a call connects -- the phone answers the request, not the
call. Four seconds, guessed, and on the server where it can be
changed rather than on the phone where it cannot.

That needed a nudge. The errand sender looks every thirty seconds,
which is right for an alarm and far too slow here: the change would
expire twenty seconds in, before the tick meant to carry it. So a
delayed change wakes the sender when its moment comes.

With no `during_url` the call still goes and he says the speaker
is beyond him -- half of what they asked for beats none of it.

**Speaker may well not work**, and Tasker says so itself: *"Google
broke the Speakerphone API for third party apps like Tasker on
Android 10 so on some devices this action might not work."* Muting
goes a different way and is unaffected. Built anyway, because the
alternative is guessing, and it will be known the first time a call
is on.

### Shall I ring him back, sir?

Owner, on the missed-call rule: *"it says you got a missed call
right -- along with that I want, do you want me to call sir?"*

The announcement should end with the offer. Saying it is the easy
part; the hard part is that the yes must not be met with the same
question again.

#### Why the obvious version does not work

A rule may only reach for tools that **do not write**, so a rule
cannot call `call_place` -- and an announcement that merely says
"shall I ring him?" leaves nothing on the server knowing a question
was asked. The yes then arrives at `call_place`, which finds no
pending call and does what it is built to do: asks.

	Jarvis: Kliffy rang at two and you have not called back.
	        Shall I ring him, sir?
	You:    yes
	Jarvis: Shall I ring Kliffy, sir?

#### call_offer, and what the gate actually rests on

`call_offer` is the asking half of `call_place` with the dialling
taken out. It records that a question is going out and nothing else,
which is why it does not write and why a rule may use it. It is
given to the **write** step rather than run before it, because the
step that decides who is outstanding is the only one that knows the
name.

And `call_place` now rings on a name alone when a question about
that same person is already pending and they have spoken since.

**That is not a loosening**, and it is worth being exact about why.
The token never was the evidence. It proves a question was *asked*,
which is the cheap half; what proves it was *answered* is that the
person has said something since -- and that check is unchanged and
still the only thing standing between a wish and a ringing phone.
The token remains the ordinary way back and still pins which person
was agreed to. It is simply no longer the only way, because
insisting on it would have somebody who was just asked "shall I ring
Kliffy?" asked it a second time.

A question agreed about one person is still never spent on another,
and an offer nobody has answered still rings nothing. Both tested.


### He types badly and it does not matter

Owner: *"you know how i prompt right .. lots of spelling mistake .. i
type something but somehow you identify what i want .. that is how
ill be typing on jarvis too .. so i want jarvis to do the right task
.. right tools must be called"*

Measured rather than assumed. `TestASentenceSurvivesItsSpelling`
asks twenty-seven of his real sentences twice, once as typed and once
spelt correctly, and compares the two answers.

	27 of 27 survived their spelling; 0 cost by it,
	0 wrong either way, 0 only right when mangled

`cal amma` reached the phone and not the calendar. `remind me in to
hours to take the washign out` set a hundred and twenty minutes. The
four cases that should call nothing called nothing, which is the
failure a tool-choice suite cannot see: a mangled sentence turning an
answer into a search.

#### Why the comparison is paired

The one hundred and twenty-five cases in `cases` are all in textbook
English, so nothing measured the input this person actually produces.
Adding mangled cases alone would not have measured it either -- a
failure would be indistinguishable from a tool description that was
weak anyway.

So each case carries its own tidy twin and only one outcome fails:
**the tidy sentence right and the tangled one wrong.** Both wrong is
logged and not failed, because the descriptions are `cases`' subject
and failing here as well reports one fault in two places.

#### What this does not cover

A misspelling is recovered from the sentence around it -- "right
tootls must be aclled" has only one word that fits. **A name has no
such redundancy**: "call Alikya" is well formed, so nothing in the
sentence contradicts it. That is what `heard.Likeness` and the
confirm step are for, and this file does not test them.

So the rule stands unchanged: guess when reading, ask when changing.
The risk was never the wrong tool. It is the right tool and the wrong
person.

## A desktop workspace client, and a design system before it

Owner's decision, 10 October 2026: a second client is to be built, a
desktop workspace for the Linux laptop -- terminals in a grid, saved
workspaces that open Chrome and VS Code, the conversation, and
notifications pushed from the server. **The design system comes
first**, before any screen, and it is to be **Jarvis style**: a
heads-up display, thin luminous lines on near-black, one accent.

The requirements are in a shared document,
[Jarvis Design System -- Requirements Spec](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/5ecf8635-3bf2-4fbb-a669-3e699239f18c),
which lists its own open questions. Until they are answered, these hold
as proposals rather than decisions: cyan as the accent, and the existing
web client in `client/` left on its own amber system.

**The desktop client is Electron, in its own repository** at
`workspace/personal-assistant-client`. Owner's decision, the same day,
after the tradeoffs were laid out. This does not reverse the Flutter
decision above, whose reason was one codebase for Android and the web;
it does not reach a Linux-only shell whose core is a terminal emulator.
What decided it was the terminals: five panes running full-screen
programs such as Claude Code need xterm.js, the emulator inside VS
Code, and node-pty. Tauri was rejected because on Linux it renders
through WebKitGTK, whose WebGL and backdrop blur are the two things
this design leans on. The costs, accepted: about 250 MB of memory, and
`client/lib/api` is rewritten in TypeScript rather than reused.

Two facts found while writing it, which constrain what comes after:

- **The laptop runs GNOME on Wayland**, so `wmctrl` and `xdotool`
  cannot place native windows. Placing Chrome and VS Code needs them
  launched under XWayland or a GNOME Shell extension.
- **`GET /v1/about` returns `[assistant] name`, without a token.**
  Added the same day for the desktop client's sign-in screen, which
  shows the name before there is a token to present. The name is not a
  secret -- the assistant says it aloud -- and it is the only thing the
  endpoint says. Empty means the assistant has none, and a client then
  shows none rather than one of its own.

**The desktop client is to hold a WebSocket to the server.** Owner's
direction, the same day: the client is a chat that should answer at
once and a place notifications are published to as they happen, and
neither should wait on the client asking. This is the case section 2
left open -- WebSocket "earns its place only if" something more than
one answer has to travel -- and it is now met: an answer, progress,
and announcements nobody asked for, over one connection, with the
client's own prompts and cancels going the other way. Typed clients
are pull-only today and there is no server-sent-events stream, so
this is new server work: an endpoint, authentication with the
client's token, and a fan-out of announcements to connected clients.
Not built.

**Built, 11 October 2026: `GET /v1/live`.** A WebSocket behind the
ordinary token check -- the client presents `Authorization: Bearer` on
the upgrade, exactly as on any request. On connecting it is sent the
latest event of each kind, then every event as it is published, as
JSON lines `{"type":"satellite","state":"listening","at":…}`; it is
pinged every 30 seconds and sends nothing yet. The first event kind is
the voice satellite's state, for the desktop client's core: a watcher
holds Home Assistant's own WebSocket open
(`subscribe_entities` on `[homeassistant] satellite`), so a state
arrives the moment Home Assistant has it rather than on a poll, and
reports `unknown` whenever Home Assistant cannot be heard, retrying from
one second to thirty. A client that falls 32 events behind is dropped
and reconnects, so no client holds up another.

- **`github.com/coder/websocket`** is the one new dependency: the
  standard library has none, and this one is small, maintained,
  context-aware and has no dependencies of its own. Both sides use it,
  the endpoint and the Home Assistant watcher.
- **Upgrades skip the request timeout.** chi's Timeout cancels a
  request's context after `[server] request_timeout`, which would cut a
  healthy live connection; `middleware.TimeoutUnlessUpgrade` applies it
  to everything else.
- The hub is in-process (`internal/app/live`), like the event bus:
  nothing here needs more than one process.

**The desktop client asks over the same connection.** Owner's direction,
11 October 2026: the chat goes through the WebSocket. The client sends
`{"type":"prompt","request":…,"conversation_id":…,"text":…}` and
`{"type":"cancel","chat_id":…}`; for each prompt it is sent `chat` when
accepted (its `request` echoed, with the chat and conversation ids),
`progress` as it works, and `answer` when it ends, with the reason and,
for a failure, the error code and detail -- or `refused`, with the reason
in words, when it was never accepted. Pieces of an answer are not sent,
as on `/api/chat` for anything but a voice turn.

- **One way of asking, two ways in.** `internal/app/asking` holds the
  five steps `/api/chat` used to do inline -- resolve the conversation,
  supersede what is running in it, store the chat, subscribe to it,
  submit it -- and both `/api/chat` and `/v1/live` call it, so neither
  can drift. `/api/chat` keeps only what is Home Assistant's: its wire
  format, its pieces of an answer, and cancelling when the caller hangs
  up.
- **A dropped connection does not cancel a typed chat.** A voice turn
  whose caller has gone is stopped, because nobody will hear it; a typed
  one runs on and its answer is in the conversation when the client
  comes back.
- A cancel is honoured only for a chat in one of the caller's own
  conversations.

**The desktop client is to be an MCP server the assistant uses.** Owner's
objective, 11 October 2026: *"we will be creating MCP for this machine
client and will be integrating with Jarvis -- it's an objective."* The
laptop's terminals, apps and spaces, which the client already holds, are
to become tools the assistant can call. A goal, not yet designed or
begun.

**Satellite pairing per client, designed and deferred.** Owner, 11 October
2026: *"design the satellite pairing per client, so a client can have both
typed and voice... a client should send whether that request is by voice or
typed"*, then *"remember it, we'll develop later"*. The fixed channel
conflates how a prompt was asked, how its answer is delivered, and whether
a screen can confirm. Proposed: each client declares what it can do at
sign-in (`screen`, `speaker`), the ceiling; each prompt says how it was
asked (`input: voice|typed`), defaulting to the client's, since Home
Assistant's Ollama-shaped request carries only the model and the messages.
A client may be paired with a satellite; the server watches every
satellite and gives a voice prompt to the one processing at that moment,
or treats it as unpaired voice when that is unclear. A paired client's
core follows its satellite, shows its voice turns, and takes their
confirmations on its screen. Open: the split itself, attribution by
timing, and confirmations on the paired screen. Not begun.

**A conversation that changes is announced, whoever asked in it.**
Owner, 11 October 2026: a question asked by voice reached the database,
but the desktop client showing that conversation did not move -- with
the WebSocket open, it should update by itself. The runner now tells the
hub whenever a conversation has something new in it: a turn starting, a
turn ending (answered, failed or stopped), and a title given. The hub
sends `{"type":"conversation","conversation_id":…}` to that
conversation's owner only, and the client fetches the list and, if it is
showing that conversation, the conversation again.

- **The runner is where it is said**, not either way of asking: every
  chat passes through it -- voice, typed, the chats API, one recovered
  after a restart -- and the title is given there too.
- **A notice is not a state.** The satellite's state is remembered and
  sent first to a client that connects, and an unchanged one is not sent
  again; a notice is neither -- two alike are two things that happened,
  and one from before a client connected is nothing it needs. Each
  carries its user, kept off the wire, and a connection is sent only its
  own caller's.
- Scale: three notices a turn (start, end, title once), each one
  conversation read to find its owner. A client fetching again after each
  folds a burst into at most two fetches.
- Not yet announced: what was said unasked, which is written to the
  conversation outside the runner.

**The words being heard are passed to the desktop clients as they are
said.** Owner, 12 October 2026: *"show the streamed words... only my
words, what I speak"*, under the core, behind a development switch in the
client. The speech bridge already streams each turn to Deepgram with
interim results; it now posts the words heard so far to
`POST /v1/speech/hearing` (`{text, final}`) whenever they change, and the
server sends them on at once as a live notice
`{"type":"hearing","text":…,"final":…}` to that user's clients only.

- **Shown, never stored.** It is a view of the microphone: a notice, not
  remembered by the hub, so a client that connects later is not sent
  old words. The turn itself is recorded when it arrives as a question.
- The text is cut from the front past 600 characters, keeping what is
  being said now. The path is logged at debug, like the health checks:
  it arrives several times a second while somebody speaks.
- Scale: a few posts a second per spoken turn, each one hub fan-out; no
  database work.
- **The wait goes with the words** (owner, 13 October 2026, in the desktop
  client: *"I want to see the timer in the box"*). The bridge ends a turn
  once no word has come for a while -- two seconds before any word, then
  a fifth of a second a word, between one and five -- and says how many
  seconds are left as `wait` on each notice: one with no words at the
  first audio, and one whenever a word starts the wait again, the words
  changed or not. The server passes it on as `"wait"`, held between 0 and
  30 seconds; a notice without one, as the final words are, carries none.

**The dashboard reads the server from two endpoints.** Owner, 11 October
2026, approving the desktop client's Home with the server's health and
the day on the right (*"both"*). `internal/app/api/home`, behind the
token like everything else:

- `GET /v1/home/server` -- `started_at`, `restarts` (systemd's NRestarts
  for the unit this process runs under, read from its own cgroup; absent
  outside systemd), `database` (`ok` or `unreachable`, a two-second
  ping), `satellite` (the live hub's latest state, now readable through
  `Hub.Latest`), `model` (the default), and `last_turn` (the caller's
  latest chat: status, channel, started and finished, seconds).
- `GET /v1/home/today` -- from now to the end of tomorrow in the person's
  zone: every calendar's events that have not ended (one under way
  stays), time-ordered, with the calendars that could not be read named;
  and the reminders due by then. `diary` says `ok`, `not_connected` (no
  Google account) or `unavailable` (it did not answer within eight
  seconds); the reminders are answered either way.
- **Only what the server can see.** The microphone's level, the last
  wake word and which speech engine the bridge fell back to live on the
  satellite's machine and never reach the server, so they are left out
  rather than guessed. Phone alarms are not stored as a list; they come
  from reminders.
- Scale: one ping, one `systemctl show` and one single-row chat read per
  `server` call; one parallel read of every calendar and one reminder
  listing per `today` call. The client asks every 30 and 60 seconds
  while Home is open -- about 3,000 calls a day of Home left open.


### The bar that kept the rules scarce forbade every remark

Owner: *"there must be a next AI pass .. its only purpose make Jarvis
talk to me, not only as reminder but also like companion ..
commenting on my taste .. and the only way is to create rules, coz
only then the server will intimate Jarvis .. so the model should
create rules based on the purpose, and the response by Jarvis should
be made based on the facts."*

The pass he was asking for already existed. `internal/app/noticing`
has read the description hourly since 9 October and written **zero
rules**: twenty-five in `jobs`, every one of kind `rule`, none
`noticed`.

Not a bug. Three lines in `judging.go` forbid exactly what he now
wants:

	Something can go wrong with it, or be missed
	Hearing it would change what they do. A remark they can do
	  nothing with is not worth an interruption.
	Say nothing where the pattern is merely interesting

A remark on somebody's taste **is** a remark they can do nothing
with, and it **is** merely interesting. The bar written to prevent
four hundred rules also forbids every companion rule there could
be. So the work was a second purpose, not a second pass.

#### Two bars, one mechanism

`Purpose` carries the judge prompt, the kind, the allowance and
whether the rule must read before it speaks. `Useful` is what was
there. `Companion` writes kind `remarked`.

The allowances are **separate**, so a week of useful rules cannot
silence every remark and a talkative week of remarks cannot crowd
out a rule that matters.

And the companion rests **a week**, not six hours. The asymmetry is
not caution about cost. A rule catching the phone failing to charge
may fire weekly and be welcome every time, because each firing is a
different fact. A companion remarking on the same person's taste
weekly is a machine performing attention, and the fourth one lands
as noise however good the first was.

#### What the companion is judged on instead

Not usefulness, which it cannot have. **Truth and specificity.**

The failure of a companion is not volume, it is flattery. A remark
assembled from something generically true about people reads as
attention and is not, and one wrong remark costs more than ten
unsaid ones: a person told something false about themselves stops
believing the true ones. So the bar refuses compliments outright --
praise from a machine is worth nothing to anybody -- refuses
guesses at what they feel or why they did something, and refuses
anything that would fit somebody else.

#### Grounded in code, not in the prompt

His second sentence was the important one. A remark written when the
rule is made and recited unchanged for months is a fortune cookie:
true in October, asserted with the same confidence in March.

So a companion rule must reach the facts at the moment it fires, and
that is checked in `Grounded(acts)` rather than asked for in the
prompt -- a lookup of its own, or a write that may call for one.
A rule that would speak without reading is refused before it is
kept. The material is there: 217 `music.state` in thirty days,
carrying track, artist and playlist.

#### Why this is not the watchers that were deleted

On 5 October `notice.Often` and `notice.Novel` went, with the
decision that nothing is said unless a sender says so. This is not
that, and the difference is the whole of why it is safe: a rule is
standing, named, carries the reason it was written, and can be
retired. A per-event guess is none of those, and could not say what
it was for.

Retirement now reads every purpose, so a remark that has stopped
earning its place can be taken back the same way.


### A marker, and the reason it had nothing to mark

Owner: *"there should be a marker .. which rule is created by AI for
its purpose, and which is created by me."*

The marker was already in the data -- `kind` is `rule`, `noticed` or
`remarked`, and the API has always sent it. The page never drew it.
It does now, on his rules only: a badge beside the name, named and
not merely coloured, because colour alone is unreadable to anyone
who cannot tell those two apart. **No badge means yours**, which is
the ordinary case and the one that should be quiet.

The label says what the rule is, `Noticed` or `Remarked`, and not
who wrote it. The assistant's name is configuration and this page
has never been told it.

#### The field the marker pointed at was being destroyed

A marker is only half of it. A rule nobody asked for has to say what
it is for, or the only thing to do with it is delete it -- and that
reason was being written into `Why`.

`Store.Ran` overwrites `why` on **every single run** with the
outcome of that run: a failed lookup, a check that withheld, nothing
at all. So the reason a rule was written survived until the first
time the rule worked, and then it was gone. Written three hours ago
and already load-bearing in two places.

Two different facts were in one column. Why it exists, which never
changes, and what happened last time, which changes every run.
Migration 52 separates them: `because` is set once and never
written again.

The allowance was reading the same column -- `HasPrefix(j.Why,
Mark)` -- which would have handed him a fresh allowance the moment
his last rule fired. It keys on `kind` alone now, and `Mark` is gone
from `Purpose` with it.

#### Unknown means theirs

`RuleAuthor` maps anything it does not recognise to the person, not
to the assistant. A rule wrongly marked as his invites somebody
deleting their own work on the strength of a label, and the two
deletions are not the same act.



### The judge was not refusing, it was failing

Owner: *"the rule writing by AI must be done hourly too, so it can
talk nice current stuffs too."*

It already was hourly, and had been: `profileEvery = time.Hour`, with
the rule pass run immediately after each description rebuild. It had
written nothing anyway.

`make evals-wondering` asks the real judge what it would write
against the real description and keeps nothing -- no rule, no
allowance spent, the writer never called. It exists because the pass
is silent by design most hours, which makes a bar that works and a
bar that can never be cleared look identical from outside.

The first run returned in 1.9 seconds for two calls on a
6,400-character prompt, which is too fast. The answer was:

	The server would not accept that request.

`slow_model = claude-sonnet-5-5` -- the model chosen for this work --
is refused by this gateway with *"Model is not supported for the
endpoint (HTTP 400)"*. Every judge call had failed for as long as it
was set.

#### Why nobody noticed for a day

A gateway refusal arrives as a *message* of kind error, not as an
error from `Run`. `Wondered` swallows an answer it cannot parse on
purpose -- a missed rule costs one unremarked pattern and a misread
one runs for ever -- so the refusal reached the pass as "nothing to
say", which is also the correct answer most hours.

Three things now make that legible:

**`make evals-models`** asks which models the gateway takes, because
it publishes no list. Measured 10 October 2026 -- accepted:
`claude-sonnet-4-6`, `claude-opus-5-5`, `claude-opus-4-6`. Refused:
`claude-sonnet-5-5`, `claude-haiku-5-5`, `claude-haiku-4-5`. The
last of those is the model the `fast_model` comment was measured
against on 2 October, so that measurement can no longer be acted on.

**`slow_model` is `claude-opus-5-5`**, which is the nearest thing to
what was asked for that this gateway will take.

**The pass says when it has nothing.** `nothing was worth a rule`,
with the purpose. Silence was the bug.

#### And what it says now that it answers

	noticed   {"nothing": "all observable patterns worth acting on
	          are already covered by the 21 rules held"}
	remarked  {"nothing": "no music or listening data was given"}

The second is **true**, and it is the next thing in the way.

#### Taste disperses, so the profile never sees it

`howOften` ranks labels by count and keeps the top `Mostly` = 12. A
label is kind plus value, so a kind with one value concentrates and a
kind with many disperses.

Measured over 28 days: 245 music events across **54 distinct
artists**, the busiest being Daft Punk at 17. Twelfth place in the
ranked list is `battery.level "34"` at 24. So music is 9.7% of
everything the devices reported and gets **none** of the twelve
lines, while `battery.level` -- one kind split into percentage
buckets, each common because the phone reports continuously -- takes
**nine of them**, to say something the prose half already says in one
sentence.

Taste is by nature many distinct values. The ranking cannot surface
it at any cap.


### A phone's rhythm applied to a laptop

Owner, on an announcement at half past midnight -- *"Your laptop has
gone quiet, sir -- nothing reported in the last forty-eight
minutes."* -- **"its unwanted statement."**

The rule was his own, `a device has gone quiet`, every five minutes.
The check behind it was right about the laptop having said nothing
for forty-eight minutes and wrong about that meaning anything.

Two faults, and neither was the threshold.

**Which devices count.** `Chatty = 5` said a device whose silence is
evidence is one that reported five times in the window. The laptop
says exactly one thing in its life -- that it joined or left a
network -- and says it in pairs five seconds apart. Six of those
inside a minute cleared a threshold meant for a phone reporting its
position every two minutes. Measured over three days: twenty-nine
reports, a median gap of **0.8 minutes** and a ninetieth percentile
of **8.8 hours**, with **twelve of its twenty-eight gaps longer than
the forty-five-minute threshold**. Its ordinary night is a fault
under that test, and would be most nights.

`Silence` was measured on the phone and says so in its own comment.
Nobody measured the laptop, and nobody should have to: the check now
asks whether *this* device had already gone this quiet while it was
working, which is a question about the evidence in hand. The same
constant, used twice -- once as the silence that is wrong, once as
the ordinary gap it must not already exceed. `Chatty` stays as a
floor against a device that reported once.

This is deliberately not a per-device table. A device that starts
reporting steadily qualifies the moment it does, with nothing
configured, and that is the whole point of measuring the device
rather than naming it.

**One outage, said five times.** On the evening of 8 October the
same silence was announced at 21:58, 22:18, 22:28, 22:38 and 23:59
-- *"forty-seven minutes"*, *"sixty-seven minutes"*, *"seventy-seven
minutes"*, *"eighty-seven minutes"*, *"three hours"*.

The engine already guards against this, and the guard was told the
truth: a rule is shown what it said last time and asked to answer
with silence if what it has now is the same news. The model was
right to speak. **The input really was different every run**, because
the check counted the minutes into its own sentence.

`situation.Found` had a `Key` for exactly this -- the device and the
hour it fell silent -- and **nothing has read it since the watcher
that did was replaced by the rule engine**. A key named for saying
one thing once, computed on every run, discarded on every run, while
the thing it promised went unhandled. It is deleted. The sentence is
the identity now, and the check says *when* the device fell silent
rather than how long ago, so one outage is one sentence for as long
as it lasts.

The general form, and the one worth carrying: **a check whose words
change while the situation does not has no guard at all.** Any
duration, count or clock reading in a situation's sentence is a
rule that will repeat itself.


### The judge was shown a list of names

Owner, in the same breath: **"the model should look at the current
rules and how useful they are, and create useful rules. It has to
question itself -- is that rule useful?"**

It could not. `Holding` handed the judge one line per rule --
`name: schedule` -- and nothing about what any of them had done.
It was deciding what to add with no way to tell a rule that works
from a rule that has never once spoken.

The record was there the whole time, in `runs`. Measured on 10
October across twenty-five rules:

| | |
|---|---|
| runs | **2,487** |
| things said | **18** |
| rules that ran and never spoke | **8 of 16** |

`somebody has been trying` had run **1,317 times** and said nothing.
`a device has gone quiet` had run **529 times** and spoken **6**, of
which five were one silence announced five times.

So `noticing.Standing` renders every rule in force with its record --
schedule, who wrote it, ran, said, and the last thing it said -- and
both passes read the same list. The judging prompt now has to hold
the rule it is about to write against it: *what will this rule's two
numbers be in a month, and would they be worth the interruptions?*

**Without ids.** The list read while deciding what to *add* carries
no identifiers, so nothing on it can be named. A judge that could
name a rule there is a judge that could be talked into naming one
for deletion, and the two decisions are deliberately different
prompts.

**Retiring now sees everything and may still only take back its
own.** That stands: rules the person asked for are theirs to keep or
drop. But it is shown theirs as context without ids, because whether
one of his own still earns its place is a question about everything
that is watching -- a rule of his gone quiet because one of theirs
now covers the same occasion reads as dead only when both are in
view.

Two things fixed in passing. `retire` filtered on
`j.Kind != noticing.Kind`, which silently excluded every
`remarked` rule from ever being reconsidered; it uses
`noticing.Mine` now. And the record is read once per pass and handed
to both, rather than each reading the table for itself.

**Live, 11 October, two minutes apart.** The last run on the old
binary spent a model call and had the model suppress the repeat:

```
why: there was nothing new to say
steps: [tool situation_find ran 1ms, write stopped 2358ms]
```

The first on the new one never got past the first step:

```
why: situation_find found nothing
steps: [tool situation_find stopped 2ms]
```

A check that refuses is cheaper than a model that declines, and it
is the only one of the two that is reliable.


### The ranking hid everything about the person

Owner: **"fix the taste ranking."**

`howOften` ranked *labels* -- the kind and the value together -- and
cut at twelve. Measured over the owner's own four weeks:

| | moments | distinct values | lines it got |
|---|---|---|---|
| `battery.level` | **1,230** | 100 percentages | **8 of 12** |
| `music.state` | 97 | **54 artists** | **0** |
| `call.received` | 24 | 10 people | **0** |

It is arithmetic, not judgement. A kind with one value puts its whole
count on one line; a kind with many spreads it across all of them. So
the widest thing about somebody is always the first to disappear, and
**no cap could have fixed it** -- raising twelve to twenty buys eight
more battery percentages before it buys a single artist.

The same fault, worse, in the section underneath. Nine of the twelve
lines of *things that happen together* were one battery discharging:
*"battery.level 38, then battery.level 37"*, *"battery.level 45, then
battery.level 47"*, and nine more of the same.

**Two changes, and the first is the deeper one.**

A value that is a number is a measurement and not a thing that
happened, so it is no part of what the moment *is*. `moment.label`
folds such a kind to its kind alone. The owner's own decision already
says this -- *a varying number is never `value`* -- and this cannot
rely on senders honouring it.

Judged **per kind and never per value**. One call came in from a
number nobody had named, and `+916746580844` parses as a number
perfectly well; it stays a caller of its own because the other values
that kind has seen are people with names. A kind is a reading only
when every value it has ever carried is a number. On the live data
that selects `battery.level` and nothing else.

Then the kind is the line, and the values sit inside it. A kind is
something a device reports -- a short list that grows a few times a
year -- where labels grow with every new artist. So the cap moved
from twelve labels to twenty kinds, with the five most frequent
values named inside each and the total beside them, because five of
fifty-four must not read as five of five.

A single value is kept rather than dropped as part of what the kind
is: somebody whose calls all come from one person is the most worth
knowing thing that kind has to say. The cost is that a sender naming
nothing says `always "unknown"`, which is true and is about the
sender.

**What the same four weeks produce now**, top of the list rather than
absent from it:

```
- music.state: 97 times, on 7 of 11 days; 54 different, most often
  "Daft Punk" (9), "Anirudh Ravichander" (5), "Jason Recht" (4)...
- battery.level: 73 times, on 8 of 11 days; readings from 2 to 99
- call.received: 24 times, on 9 of 11 days; 9 different, most often
  "Amma" (7), "Alekhya Chintada" (6)...
- bluetooth.connected: 12 times, often around 8pm; always "bike helmet"
```

`battery.level` fell from 1,230 moments to 73 without a single event
being dropped: with the percentage out of the label, a phone
reporting every few minutes collapses under the two-hour rule that
was already there and always should have applied to it.

**`make evals-rhythm`** prints that block from the real database and
calls no model. It exists because a made-up fixture cannot find this
class of fault: the old ranking passed every test it had, each built
from a handful of events by hand. The fault only appears at the ratio
real devices report at -- one sensor talking a thousand times against
a person listening a hundred -- and that ratio is in the database and
nowhere else.

Left alone: *things that happen together* is still led by the screen
and the battery, which do genuinely co-occur. The nine lines of one
battery falling are gone, and that was the part that was wrong.


### The pass was never called

Having fixed the ranking, I watched for the next hourly pass to see
what the companion made of taste it could finally read. The
description was rewritten. **Nothing followed it.** No judge call, no
*nothing was worth a rule*, no warning -- the pass simply did not
happen.

Counted across the log: **34 descriptions written, 3 passes run.**

```go
var thinkingUp func(context.Context, string)   // line 619, nil

watching.Add(1)
go func() {
    describeDaily(remindCtx, chats, describing, thinkingUp, ...)
}()

// ... 130 lines of setup ...

thinkingUp = noticed(scheduled, ranLog, ...)   // line 751
```

The goroutine captures the *variable*, but it reads it the instant it
starts, which is microseconds later and a hundred and thirty lines
too early. `describeDaily` takes the nil, and `if noticed != nil`
skips the pass for the life of the server.

And it is a race, which is why it was not obvious: on three
restarts out of thirty-four the scheduler let the setup reach line
751 before the goroutine's first statement, and those are the three
passes that ran. Same binary, same configuration, different
behaviour per restart -- including twice in the same hour while this
was being diagnosed.

Everything found before this was real and none of it was the cause.
The gateway was refusing `claude-sonnet-5-5`; the useful bar did
forbid every remark; the judge was shown a list of names. All true,
all fixed, and **on thirty-one evenings in thirty-four no model was
ever asked anything.**

The fix is to start the loop after the thing it needs exists. The
comment that justified the old order -- *"the goroutine that uses it
starts before the jobs store is built"* -- was describing the bug as
though it were a constraint. Nothing needs that loop running in the
first ten minutes; `profileFirst` is ten minutes.

And `describeDaily` now says so at startup when it is handed nothing:

```
the description will be rewritten but nothing will be noticed from it
```

**The lesson is the same one as two sections above, in a third
place.** A silent skip and a considered decision not to act are
indistinguishable from outside, and the cheapest way to lose days is
to let them look alike. *A thing that can be switched off must say
so when it is off.*


### It has to ask itself before it speaks

Owner: **"if the model is going to comment, or say something, it
should ask itself a question -- whether it is actually useful, or
does it make sense. Same goes for rule writing too."**

Rule writing already asks it, and now asks it against the record of
what every rule in force has done. The firing did not. A write step
opened with *"You are writing one sentence to be said out loud,
now"*, spent four paragraphs on how to phrase it, and offered
silence in one clause at the very end.

A model told at length how to word something will word something.
Measured: `a device has gone quiet` spoke six times in 529 runs,
which sounds careful until the six are read -- five were one silence
announced five times in two hours, and the sixth was a laptop being
quiet at half past midnight. **Every one of them passed a step whose
last line offered silence.**

So the step now opens by saying that the deciding is the job and the
sentence is only what follows if the answer is yes, and `worthSaying`
puts the two questions in the owner's own words before the answer
format.

**Two bars and not one, which is the part that needed care.** The
first draft asked "is it useful?" of everything, and that would have
undone the companion the day it shipped: *a thing they can do
nothing about is not worth an interruption* is exactly what keeps
