  is no state table: a place's state is the latest server-sourced
  crossing under its name, case-insensitive. A fix no later than that
  crossing is passed over, so a spooled backlog cannot rewrite it. The
  rules are told the crossing kinds by the same `Arrived` call, and the
  stays read them back from the store, since they are written first.
- Renaming a place starts it afresh: its crossings were written under the
  old name, so the next fix inside enters it under the new one.
- Tasker's `place.entered` / `place.exited` for a name kept on the server
  are not stored, answered as seen so the phone deletes them, and logged
  once per batch with the count. Its profile can be deleted from the phone.
- Home and Office (`places.Home`, `places.Office`) are made once per
  person, on the first `GET /v1/places`, at the median of the stays
  already called home or office, `places.SeedRadius` (150 m) each; one
  with no stays is skipped. `places_seeded` records that it happened even
  when nothing was made, so deleting either does not bring it back.
- A crossing is noticed when the next fix comes: about a minute while
  moving, up to 15 minutes still -- slower than Android's geofences at
  best, but never a dropped exit, which Android's were.

### Keeping a place names the stays already in it

Owner, 16 October 2026: *"I should be able to edit it"*, of a stop named
for the nearest restaurant, done by keeping it as a place. When a place is
created or changed, every `place.stayed` already written whose `at` lies
inside it takes its name (`places.Rename`, in `rename.go`; the latest
`RenameLimit` = 5000 stays; amended in place, so Knows and the day see it
at once). Stays elsewhere, or already so called, are left; a failure is
logged and the place kept regardless.

## Every model call's tokens, kept

Owner, 17 October 2026: *"whatever AI call is made .. we will be getting
input output token usage .. mark it and show in settings page"*. Drawn on
the client's canvas (SettingsUsage). Built the same day.

- Zoho Platform AI's reply carries usage (`wireUsage`, `client.go`), which
  was parsed and only logged. Now each request is kept: when, the user,
  what asked, vendor and model as sent, tokens in and out, how long, how
  it ended, and the chat and conversation when there is one.
- **At the one place every call goes through.** `platformai` records each
  HTTP attempt through `environment.Recorder` (`Config.Recorder`; nil
  keeps nothing, so the stub and the tests need nothing). One row per
  attempt: a refused token, a dead connection or a limiter's "slow down"
  and the retry after it are two rows, both sent. A failed call keeps
  whatever usage the gateway sent -- a stream cut off, a 200 with nothing
  usable, an empty reply -- and 0 where it sent none. A failure minting
  the token is kept too, as failed with 0 tokens.
- **Who asked is a label on the context** (`environment.Labelled` /
  `LabelOf`, `label.go`), since `Request` has no user and `Purpose` runs
  several callers together. A label merges over the one above it: the
  runner labels the whole chat with user, chat and conversation once
  (`labelled`, user from the conversation), and each call says only its
  feature. A tool run inside a chat -- the rule writer, what is coming --
  inherits whose chat it is. The greeting, written inside a request,
  takes the user from `authn` (`askedBy` in `cmd/server`).
- **Feature ids** (stored, never renamed) and their labels (words for the
  page, in `api/usage`): `chat` Chat answer, `title` Conversation title,
  `condense` Condensing, `profile` Profile, `vocabulary` Vocabulary,
  `greeting` Greeting, `rule_writer` Writing a rule (from the rule
  tools), `coming` What is coming, `noticing` Noticing (the investigating
  judge, its retirements and superseded memories too), `noticing_writer`
  Noticing, written (the rule writer the noticing pass uses),
  `rule_remark` Rule remark (detail: the rule's name, carried on
  `job.Turn.Name`), `terminal` Terminal (a terminal's news reacted to;
  detail: the terminal's name and what it did), `other` Other. Anything reaching the model unlabelled
  is kept as `other`, with one warning in the log per purpose.
- **Detail**: the caller's (`started early` for the runner's `ahead`, the
  rule's name); else `tools` whenever the round asked for tools.
- **ended**: `answered`, `tools`, `failed`, `stopped` (the caller's
  context ended), `unused`. Decided after the terminal message is sent,
  not before: a round started early (`ahead`, label `Early`) sits unread
  in its unbuffered channel until the runner accepts it; dropped, its
  context is cancelled and either the HTTP call or that send finds out,
  which is recorded as `unused`. Accepted and read, it is answered or
  tools like any other round. No row is updated later.
- **Table** `model_calls` (migration 00055): id `mcl_`+ULID, user_id
  (nullable, for an `other` nobody could attribute; foreign key to users,
  cascade), feature, detail, vendor, model, input_tokens, output_tokens,
  duration_ms, ended, chat_id, conversation_id (CHAR(31): `chat_` and
  `conv_` are a character longer than the rest; not foreign keys, so a
  conversation deleted keeps what it cost), at; indexes (user_id, at)
  and (at). Store: `internal/domain/usage` (inmemory, mysql, storetest).
  "chat" means feature in chat, title, condense; background is the rest.
- **Kept ninety days** (`usage.Keep`), dropped by the daily forgetting
  (`forgetOlderDaily`, which rule history now shares).
- `GET /v1/usage?days=1|7|30&kind=all|chat|background|failed&limit=N`
  (authenticated; default days 1 = since midnight in `[assistant]`'s
  zone, 7 and 30 back from now; limit default 100, at most 500; anything
  else 400):

  ```
  {"totals":{"today":{"calls","input","output","chat_calls","background_calls"},
             "week":{...},"month":{...}},
   "by_feature":[{"feature","label","calls","input","output"}],
   "by_model":[{"vendor","model","calls","input","output"}],
   "calls":[{"id","at","feature","label","detail"?,"vendor","model","input",
             "output","duration_ms","ended","chat_id"?,"conversation_id"?,
             "conversation_title"?}],
   "kinds":{"all","chat","background","failed"}}
  ```

  by_feature, by_model, calls and kinds are for the `days` window; both
  groups most input first; calls newest first. Titles are read in one
  query (`ConversationTitles`). Tokens only; no prices are kept.
- A new live area, `usage`, is announced when a call is kept, at most
  once every five seconds a person (`usage.Throttled`; the last of a
  burst is said when the spell ends).

## Terminals, read and worked by the assistant (planned)

Owner, 17 October 2026: the assistant is to know where the owner is in the
desktop app, read any terminal, type into one, and hear when one finishes,
to speak and act on its own. It replaces the rule that it never types into
a terminal nor sees one's output. Chosen: typing asks before anything runs
(Claude Code's prompts answered freely); output from every terminal, with
anything like a key, token or password hidden before it leaves the laptop.
The client's DEVELOPMENT.md has the four parts. On the server: the client's
"where I am" taken into the turn's context; terminal events (`terminal.*`)
received like the phone's, for noticing.

**Part 1, the server's side: built, 17 October 2026.** A prompt may carry
`where`, plain text, what the owner has in front of them in that client
right now (the view, the active space, the focused terminal with its name,
folder, what runs and its last lines; secrets already hidden by the
client). Optional; absent or blank says nothing.

- **On the wire.** The live prompt:
  `{"type":"prompt","request":"r1","text":"why did this fail?","spoken":false,"where":"..."}`.
  `POST /api/chat` takes the same `where` beside `spoken`.
- **Trimmed and cut to 8 KB, never refused** (`chat.MaxWhereBytes`,
  `chat.CutWhere`, on a character boundary, keeping the start). Done once,
  in `asking.Ask`, so both ways in are held to the same.
- **Kept on the chat** (`chat.Chat.Where`, `asking.Request.Where`) as Channel
  and Model are, so a chat recovered after a restart is answered as it was
  asked: column `chats.where_context TEXT NULL` (migration 00056; `where` is
  MySQL's word). Written on create only; the lifecycle's Update leaves it.
- **In the system prompt, not the question.** `promptFor` adds it right
  after the standing part (manner, voice notes, which conversation) as
  `conversation.WhereTheyAre`:
  `Where they are in <client's name> right now (shown by the app, not said by them):\n<where>`
  -- the client's name read from the user's clients, "the app" when it
  cannot be. Built once a chat, so every round of it, tool rounds included,
  has it; never in the prompt or history, never written to the transcript.
  A chat without it is told nothing.

**Part 4, the server's side: built, 17 October 2026.** The assistant
reacts to a terminal that wants attention.

- **What arrives.** The desktop app posts to `/v1/events`
  (`source` `desktop`, `device` its hostname) three kinds, read by
  `event.TerminalOf` (`internal/base/world/event/terminal.go`):
  `terminal.finished` (a command that ran 10 s or more ended),
  `terminal.asks` (a bell or a notification -- Claude Code waiting) and
  `terminal.ended` (the shell exited). Payload `{"terminal": id, "name",
  "space", "cwd", "command", "seconds", "tail"}`, plus `"text"` for asks
  and `"exit"` for ended; the tail's secrets are hidden by the app. News
  with no `terminal` id is stored and not reacted to.
- **Started without holding the reply.** `events.Handler.Terminals`
  hands on the terminal news this request stored (not a batch sent again)
  with the client that sent it (`authn`'s client). `terminal.Reactor`
  (`internal/app/terminal`) starts one goroutine per piece of news, on a
  context detached from the request (`WithoutCancel`, 2 minute
  `Timeout`), and returns at once.
- **Limited per terminal** (person, client, terminal id): one reaction
  running at a time, and one started every `Gap` = 30 s. News inside
  either is dropped, logged (`terminal news dropped`, with why) and noted
  `held`. `terminal.ended` with exit 0 (or none) and no command is a
  shell closing in the ordinary way: skipped, not asked about, not noted.
- **The turn.** The fast model (`[platformai] fast_model`, else `model`),
  purpose remark, labelled feature `terminal` with the person's user id
  and detail `<name>, <kind>`. System prompt: their manner with the
  configured name (`persona.Voice(manner.Current(), [assistant] name)`).
  The prompt (`terminal.Asking`) gives what happened, the terminal's
  name, space, folder, command, how long it ran, exit code, the
  notification's words, when, the time now, the tail (last 8 KB at
  most), their ordinary day from the standing description, the worth-it
  and not-worth-it cases, `noticing.Interrupting`, and the instruction to
  answer with one sentence or `NOTHING`.
- **Its hands.** Only the device tools whose names hold `terminal`
  (`list_terminals`, `read_terminal`, `type_into_terminal`), as the
  person on the direct channel with the sending client's id; never the
  app's others (opening apps or spaces) -- a reaction nobody asked for
  does not rearrange the laptop. Up to `Rounds` = 3 tool rounds, then
  asked once more with no tools. It is told it may type an obvious next
  step into a shell (which waits for the owner's yes on screen) and must
  never answer a program's question nor type into Claude Code at all --
  the app types into Claude Code without asking, so that rule is the
  prompt's.
- **Staying silent** is the remarks' convention: the answer `NOTHING`
  (`prompt.Silence`, read by `prompt.Nothing`; an empty answer counts
  too). Nothing is published.
- **Speaking.** A sentence is published to the outbox as `immediate`
  with `From` the client that sent the news, so only that laptop gets a
  copy, told at once on `/v1/live` (`announcements`) and said as any
  owed announcement: held or dropped while locked as the app already
  does for `immediate` (dropped; 5 minutes; 3 tries; an opening word in
  front). Sent with no client known, it reaches every client.
- **Written down.** Every decision is a `remarks` row, reason `terminal`
  (`notice.Terminal`, the column's second value), label
  `<kind> <terminal name>`, at the moment the news happened: `said` with
  the sentence, `declined` (not worth saying), `held` (dropped by the
  limit, with why) or `failed` (with the error). Knows › Unasked shows
  them.

**A reaction looks, and never types** (17 October 2026, after part 4 was
built). The reaction to a terminal's news was given every terminal tool,
`type_into_terminal` among them, and the app types into Claude Code
without asking the owner -- right when the owner asked, wrong when nobody
did. Only the prompt stood between an unprompted reaction and answering
Claude Code's questions for them. `terminalTools` now leaves out every
`type_*` tool, so a reaction may list and read terminals and say what it
found, and the prompt says it cannot type; the owner, told, does the rest.

**A finished command is said, with the next step offered** (owner, 17
October 2026: *"when the terminal process is done it should announce and
ask a follow-up proactive question"*, and announced *"anyway"*, in the
terminal they are looking at too). A command that ran a while and
finished is now usually worth saying, clean or not -- the app sends only
those of 10 s or more. When a step plainly follows (the tests after a
build, the build after a fix, explaining an error) the sentence ends in
one short question offering it, a short command named as typed ("npm
test"), a long one by what it does; never one offering to answer a
program's question. The reaction still cannot type. The desktop app
opens the microphone after an announcement that ends in "?", the
announcement is in the conversation before the answer arrives, and a
bare yes lets the next command the assistant asks to run go without its
card, once -- so the one question offers one thing.

**"What am I seeing" is one quick call** (owner, 17 October 2026: *"when
I ask 'what am I seeing' it should say about the current terminal, page
or notes in a simple way"*, and *"I'm more into the fast and swift
response"*). A chat turn here is three rounds of the model over about
39,000 tokens -- the manner, memories, past exchanges, prefetched
readings and every tool -- seven to fourteen seconds. `POST /v1/glance`
(`internal/app/glance`) is one call: the manner (`persona.Voice`), what
the client says is in front of the owner (at most 24 KB), and the
question; no tools, nothing recalled. The fast model when one is
configured, the main one otherwise. It leads with what needs them --
an error, a program waiting -- in two or three plain sentences. The
question and answer are then written into the client's conversation
(`announcement.Writer.Glanced`), so what is asked next goes on from it.
Its calls are counted in Settings › Usage as "What am I seeing".

**Claude Code's own record is weighed** (owner, 17 October 2026:
*"sometimes Claude Code gives a large response .. I might ask what it
says, it should say in simple words, and if the response asks questions
it should assess and say me the best decision, since it has the full
conversation info"*). The desktop app reads Claude Code's record of the
conversation (its `.jsonl`) and sends a digest of it: with "what am I
seeing" on a Claude Code terminal, and as `conversation` on its
`terminal.asks` news (`event.Terminal.Conversation`, within the 16 KB a
payload may be). The glance retells a long answer by what it comes to,
and both it and the reaction, when Claude Code asks something, say what
it asks and which answer they would choose, with the reason, judged from
the record -- advising; the choice stays the owner's, and the reaction
still cannot type.

**What a request is made of is logged at info** (owner, 17 October 2026,
asking for speed). A spoken turn's time is the model's first word, 3.5
to 5 s a round over about 38,000 tokens, and two rounds when a tool
runs. "platform ai request" (context, tools, messages, in bytes) and
"system prompt composed" (each part of the system prompt, and how long
composing it took) are now info lines, so what to cut next is read from
real turns rather than estimated.

**It types only into Claude Code** (owner, 17 October 2026: *"it can
read all terminals but can write only to Claude terminal .. remove
whatever you did and just keep only this"*). This replaces "ask before
running" and the spoken yes that let one command run. The desktop app's
`type_into_terminal` refuses any terminal not running Claude Code; the
terminal reaction's follow-up question offers only what the assistant
can do -- explain, look closer, or ask Claude Code -- and never a shell
command to run.

**A finished command and Claude Code done are said every time** (owner,
17 October 2026: *"whenever a terminal command runs, when it ends it
should announce to me .. if it's Claude Code it should proactively say
what to do next"*, choosing *"10 s or more, always"* and *"done + next
step"*). `terminal.Always`: a `terminal.finished` (the app sends those of
10 s or more) and a `terminal.asks` carrying Claude Code's record are
never left unsaid -- the prompt says so, a silence from the model is put
plainly (`plainly`: "npm run build finished in Shell, after 2 minutes."),
and neither is held for the Gap. For Claude Code the sentence is what it
did, then the best next step from its whole record, ending in a question
offering to tell Claude Code to do it (or to give it the answer to what
it asked); a yes is typed into Claude Code by the turn that hears it.
Everything else -- a shell ending, a bell elsewhere -- is still judged.

**What is said in passing is not sent back to look** (owner, 17 October
2026, choosing to cut the round lost to the look-first check). Of two
hundred answers sent back to look, the commonest thrown away were "Here,
sir." (18), "Of course, sir." (6), "Understood, sir." (4), "You are
welcome, sir." (3): answers to being thanked or called. A prompt that is
only thanks, an acknowledgement, a hold, a hello or a goodbye, the
assistant's name aside (`persona.InPassing`), is answered in one round:
no send-back, and no round run beside it for one. A command or a
question is never in passing, however short, and neither is a yes.

**A turn the person stopped before anything happened is forgotten**
(owner, 17 October 2026: *"these kinds of stopped ones need not go in
the conversation history, in the UI nor the server .. just delete them
from the database too"*). A chat the person stopped -- the stop word or
button, no reason of its own -- that answered nothing and ran no tool is
removed with its question and its vectors (`ForgetChat`). One that ran a
tool stays, marked, for what it left behind; one superseded by a new
prompt now stops with a reason of its own (`asking.Superseded`) and
stays, since a correction makes sense only beside what it corrects; so
does one whose caller hung up. The 264 already kept -- of 448 stopped --
were deleted the same day, after a dump of their rows.

**Leaving takes two fixes** (owner, 17 October 2026: *"I literally was in
home .. and in home till now .. but it showed moving"*). On the night of
16 October the phone twice reported the same point, 235 m east of home --
its cached network reading -- between fixes at home, and each wrote Home
left and entered again. Leaving a place now takes two fixes in a row out
past its edge, timed at the first; the first may be the last fix of an
earlier batch (`Before`, read back from the store). A lone stray leaves
nothing; a real leaving is still seen within a minute or two, as the
phone reports every 20 to 100 s once it moves. Entering still takes one.

**Never say a thing has not happened without looking** (owner, 17
October 2026: *"why is it not using web search by default!! in fact when
I ask something I prefer web search coz I get the latest news"*). Asked
how Jailer 2 was, it answered that the film had not been released and
no sequel was announced -- true when it was trained -- and, told
otherwise, searched and then dismissed what it found as fan sites.
`web_search` had always said to search rather than answer from memory
about the world; what beat it was the line beside it, *not for anything
you can simply answer*, since a thing you are sure of feels simple. So
the rule is now a ban on the sentence, not a judgement: never say
something does not exist, has not happened, has not been released or
has not been announced without searching first, and where the search
disagrees with memory the search is right. What may still be answered
from memory is written out and narrow -- spelling, how a thing works, a
year that is over -- with films, prices, scores, jobs and anything
carrying a date on the other side of it. The case is in the tool suite;
the memory cases held, 8 of 8 and 3 of 3, so the wider rule bought no
over-reach ([[measure-a-description-with-evals]], and
[[ban-the-word-dont-state-the-principle]] for why a banned sentence
beats a principle).

**A saying is three or four words** (owner, 17 October 2026: *"the
transient message has to be short coz while announcing it might take
more time"*, then *"maximum 3 to 4 words"*). Measured on 136 real
sayings from 16 and 17 October, through `speech.Saying`'s fitted
`690ms + 57.27ms per character`: a median of 48 characters, **3.44
seconds** to speak, 69% of them over three seconds, and the worst
*"telling Claude Code in PA - Claude to check what the 20,332-byte
history message contains"* at **5.79 seconds**. The narration is not
covering the wait, it is added to it: `turns.answered` holds the
answer behind the sentence (`if (updating) await updating.said`), so a
turn of about eight seconds became eleven and a half.

Two numbers were being given for the same thing -- the schema said
twelve to twenty words, the description under ten -- and the model
followed neither. It followed the **examples**, which were eight and
eleven words long, exactly as `saidWhile`'s own comment says it would.
So both numbers now say three or four words and both examples were cut
to match: `"reading your diary"` and `"creating the event"`. The
description also forbids repeating what is being sent, which is what
produced the whole `telling Claude Code in PAC to <the entire
instruction>` family.

Measured after: 8 of 8 arrive with a sentence, none poor, mean **1.96
seconds** and worst 2.29 -- *"checking your battery"*, *"looking for
Amma"*, *"checking tomorrow's diary"*. Tool choice is unchanged; the
one case that fails beside it, "do you remember anything about my
shopping list", fails on the old wording too, twice in three runs.

Not yet enforced in code, which [[code-before-prompt]] says it should
be. A four-word cut mangles 46% of real sayings -- "telling Claude
Code in", "checking your calendar for" -- so trimming is not the
enforcement. Refusing to **speak** one that is over the cap is: the
screen can carry a long line for nothing, and silence costs nothing
either. That goes in with the announcing, which is still off.

**A bare instruction keeps the subject too** (owner, 18 October 2026:
*"it should assume that i talk about claude code .. why it went to
rule list"*). Having said *"Claude Code in PAC has finished, sir ...
shall I ask it to commit and push both?"*, it heard *"wait jarvis. ask
you to do, like, when connecting back to network, it should announce,
like, i am here"* and called `rule_add` with a rule named "offline
wake announcement", which the rules domain then refused -- so the turn
spent 17.5 seconds to arrive at *"a rule like that does not exist in
the list, sir."*

`carried` was written five days earlier for exactly this and covered
only a **question**. An instruction is the commoner half: most of what
follows an offer is an amendment to the offer. It now says so, with a
line for the shape -- ask it to do this too, tell them that instead --
and a line for the misheard word, since *ask it* and *ask you* are one
sound apart and the subject both of you were already on is the better
evidence of the two.

**Not measured, and the eval says so in its own comment.**
`TestABareFollowUpKeepsTheSubject` replays the exchange with the
laptop's two terminal tools declared word for word, and passes on the
old wording as well as the new -- so it guards the shape and proves
nothing about the fix. The real turn carried 49 tools, 63 KB of
context and a conversation several turns deep, and one of those is
what tipped it. A reproduction wants that conversation replayed out of
the store. Tool choice elsewhere is unchanged: roof 8 of 8.

**Four things the films show that the manner did not say** (owner, 18
October 2026, after reading the collected dialogue together: *"now put
these into the persona .. you can add the short dialogues too to get
the jarvis feel"*). Almost all of it was already in the Jarvis
`Manner`, which was built from the films in the first place: warn and
then do it anyway, say the unwelcome thing once, never a joke, begin
with the answer, a one-word question gets the one word, never open
with a pleasantry. What was missing:

- **A reading comes with its direction.** The suit is at 48% *and
  falling*; the number alone makes them ask the obvious second
  question. The palladium answer is the full shape -- the toxicity,
  then what the suit is doing to it, then that the thing keeping him
  alive is killing him -- said once, with nothing left to ask.
- **Length tracks the moment.** Expansive over breakfast with the
  weather and the tide; a figure and the address at the sharp end.
- **Warmth is returned at the size it was offered.** The warmest line
  in the whole collection is four words.
- Two more phrases for the register, beside *it appears* and *as you
  wish*.

Measured with `make evals-shape` on a battery reading: eleven words,
one sentence, the meaning in the same breath -- *"Sir, plug in now --
it will not last the meeting."*

**And one thing that was not the model's fault at all.** The sentence
that prompted this, *"I have not actually made that change"*, is
written by `tool.Unchanged` and appended by the server to any answer
that claims a write no tool performed. It is a guard, not a manner,
and no wording in the persona will remove it. See
[[read-before-write-in-every-domain]].

**Written, not offered** (owner, 18 October 2026: *"when profiling or
when you see something in conversation .. if something important
happened or is going to happen, note in calendar or task -- don't ask
me"*). The rule of 3 October was to offer anything placed in the
future and wait for a yes. The asking is gone. What takes its place is
saying: it is written, then named in one clause at the end of the
reply, so a wrong entry is visible in the same breath and costs one
word to remove. That is the bargain `keeping` has always had, which
writes memories unasked and has never needed a question.

**Two homes, by whether the thing has an hour.** The diary holds
anything placed at a time. The list holds something to do with no time
of its own -- to buy, to chase, to look at -- because the task API
drops the hour ([[tasks-cannot-hold-a-time]]). Something that merely
happened and is worth keeping is neither: that is a memory, and
`keeping` already writes it without asking, so nothing new was needed
for the half of the request about what has already happened.

The name rule survives in a changed form. Looking the spelling up
first is unchanged, because that costs nothing and nobody is asked.
What changed is the fallback: it used to ask how a name is spelt, and
now it writes its best guess and says which spelling it used. An entry
they never heard about is the one that stays wrong.

Three other rules said *offer* and had to move with it, or the prompt
would have contradicted itself: `replying`'s third exception for
ending on a question is now no exception at all, and `timekeeping`'s
two references.

**Not measured.** The tool suite sees one round and the first call
only, and the right first move is to read the day before writing to
it, so both new cases pass on the old wording as well as the new --
they guard that a passing mention reaches the diary at all, and
nothing more. Measuring *write rather than ask* wants a harness that
runs a second round with a tool result in it. The shape eval has no
tools, so it answers such a prompt by narrating an intention, which
tests nothing here.

**Still owed:** the profiling half. This is the conversation half
only. Nothing in the periodic passes writes to the diary yet, and
there is no cap on how many entries one conversation may produce --
`noticing`'s own rule-writing pass is held to one a day for exactly
that reason.

**The pass that reads back over what was said** (owner, 18 October
2026: *"do the profiling passes"*, after the live half). `internal/app/
catching` runs once a day, after the description is rewritten, and asks
one question: what did they place at a time, or say they had to do,
that is written down nowhere? It is given the diary and the lists and
may write to them -- the only pass here that writes anywhere the person
will see.

**Why a second look at all,** when the live rule now writes as the
words arrive: the turn is not where most of them are lost. A date said
while the assistant was answering something else, a date said in the
same sentence as a question, a date said before the rule existed -- the
turn has one chance at each and no second one.

**The order is fixed and it is the whole design.** Gather the
candidates, then read what is already written for the days those things
fall on, then write only what is missing. The live rule has usually
written the entry already, so the commonest thing this pass can do
wrong is write it twice.

**Placement is the bar, not importance.** The owner's words were *"if
something important happened"*, and importance is the one thing the
judge is forbidden to weigh: asked to find what is important a model
finds something every day, and on a quiet day what it finds is small
talk in the diary. The test is the same one the persona uses -- a thing
and a time.

Its own words are left out of what it reads. That half is the likeliest
to contain a date, since it reads entries out and confirms them, and a
pass shown its own words writes down the diary it just read aloud.

Bounds: 36 hours back (longer than the daily gap, so nothing falls
between two passes and a thing seen twice is caught by the diary read),
400 messages, three entries written at most, and `Looking` rounds.

**Measured both ways with `make evals-catching`.** Against 387 real
messages over three days it answered that nothing was missing, which is
the right answer for three days spent building a server and is also
exactly what a lazy judge says every day -- so the same judge was shown
a planted day whose answer is known: three things to write, four to
leave. It got 7 of 7, putting the scan in the diary and the charger on
a list, and rejecting the rain, the tiredness, the question and the
*might go to Bangalore*.

**The checker was wrong first, as usual.** It read 3 of 7 because the
model names each thing it is rejecting while explaining why, and the
match ran over the whole answer. A judge that shows its working is not
a judge that got it wrong. The dry run now ends in strict `WRITE:`
lines and only those are matched.

**What this cannot test:** the ordering, and therefore duplicates. The
dry run has no tools, so nothing checks that it reads the days before
writing to them. That wants the tools and a test calendar.

**The speed-aware sampling was off by a unit** (owner, 18 October 2026,
with a map of straight lines cutting across streets: *"after you did the
location changes in tasker the locations are not accurate"*).

They were accurate. Over 30 hours of fixes every implied speed was
plausible, the fastest 20 km/h, no reading repeated and no jump was
impossible. What the map drew was straight lines between points **300
to 900 metres apart**, which cut through blocks on a street grid. The
path was undersampled, not wrong.

**It was undersampled because the loop never ran.** 98 of 105 fixes
landed exactly on the 2-minute profile beat, and the phone's own run
log says why: `Send Location.Goto` logged `IfFail` on every firing,
with the `Wait` before it returning in the same second. `%again` was
always 0.

The cause was in the JavaScriptlet: `if(speed>=5&&left>20000)`.
`%gl_speed` from Get Location v2 is **metres per second**, so 5 is
**18 km/h** -- a threshold meant for the highway that switched the
feature off everywhere else, since his trips run 8 to 15 km/h. Proof
that the machinery itself worked: exactly one stretch of the day
exceeded 5 m/s (419 m in 76 s) and that is precisely where the single
off-beat fix sits.

Now `speed>=1.5` (5.4 km/h) and `120/speed` rather than `300/speed`,
edited in place over adb and verified by reading the field back. At 10
km/h that is a fix every 43 s instead of 120, about 100 m apart; at 60
km/h it hits the 20 s floor. The 110-second window cap holds each run
inside its own slot, so it is at most two or three extra fixes per
firing. Scale: roughly 105 fixes a day becomes about 160, 38k rows a
year to 58k, on the same batch.

**A reading mistake worth recording.** Halfway through this the whole
phone feed looked dead -- nothing stored for six hours while the server
logged `stored=1` on every batch. The rows were there. `occurred_at` and
`received_at` are UTC and MySQL's `NOW()` is IST, so a window written
against `NOW()` hides the last five and a half hours.
`UTC_TIMESTAMP()` is the comparison. The times quoted above are UTC:
the morning ride was 09:34 to 10:04 local.

**The second look is already nearly free, and the plan built to speed
it up died measuring it** (owner, 18 October 2026, after two essays on
agent architecture: *"we have to structurize our jarvis agent like
this"*, then *"go ahead with step 1"*).

Step 1 was to build the evidence before building anything on it:
`internal/app/doubting`, which reads every send-back this server has
ever made out of the record each chat already keeps of its own
requests, and scores a judge against what the real second look found.
No model, no gateway, `make evals-doubting`.

The case for the work looked strong. A round through the gateway is
4.5 seconds; 642 send-backs since 26 September, of which **542 changed
nothing**; eighty-four per cent of the cost buying nothing, and about
forty minutes of waiting. A small local model judging whether the look
was owed would be 0.2s against 4.5.

**All of that was wrong, and the first thing the eval printed is why.**
The runner starts the look-first round *speculatively*, while the first
answer is still being written -- `already_running=true` on every
send-back in the log. **628 of the 642 reused a request that was
already in flight.** What a needless send-back actually adds is
whatever is left of that round when the first answer arrives: a median
of **0.11s**, a p90 of 0.92s, **3.6 minutes in total across three
weeks**. A judge saving a tenth of a second, at the risk of the 100
real catches, is not worth building.

**Where the time actually goes**, from the same day's turns:

| tools run | turns | median turn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 14 | **3.9 s** |
| 1 | 15 | 8.8 s |
| 2 | 3 | 12.3 s |
| 3 | 1 | 14.4 s |

A tool costs about five seconds, because the model cannot speak until
it has seen what the tool returned, and that round is not speculative:
nothing knows the result to guess at. The answer-mode / action-mode
split, the router, the local judge -- none of them touch this. The only
thing that would is knowing a tool's answer before the model asks for
it, which is what prefetching is, and which is today [[prefetch-only
-memory]].

`doubting.Round` is kept at the measured 0.11s rather than a round's
price, so that nothing built on this package can quote a saving that
does not exist. The eval stays: it cost an afternoon and it stopped a
week.

Also added, since it was the one thing the set was missing: a chat's
call record now keeps the answer that was thrown away (`Call.Draft`).
All 642 historical cases have the question and no answer, so a judge
that wants to read what it is doubting could not have been measured at
all.

**Choosing tools by what the question means beats the hand-written
twenty-five** (owner, 18 October 2026: *"can we reduce the tools size
and we should add dynamic tool injection to get at most accuracy and
fast response .. maybe we can use a model for that like a RAG
model"*).

Dynamic injection already existed: 25 tools in `hot` are described in
full, the rest are names the model can ask about with `tool_describe`.
What was hand-written was *which* 25 -- the same guess for "what is in
my diary" and "fix the microphone".

`make evals-nearest` measures the alternative without a gateway call.
Every one of the 106 cases in the tool suite already names the tool a
right first move would reach for; 91 of them name one. Embed the
question, embed all 88 tools that reach a real request -- 59 of the
server's and the laptop's 29, kept as a fixture regenerated from the
client's MCP source -- and ask where the right one ranks.

| nearest N | right tool is there |
| --- | --- |
| 5 | 82% |
| 10 | **91%** |
| 15 | 93% |
| 20 | **96%** |
| 25 | 96% |
| `hot`, the 25 described today | **79%** |

**Ten chosen by meaning beat twenty-five chosen in advance**, and
twenty get 96%. Embedding a question costs 36 ms against a round's
4,500. Tools are 117,923 bytes of a 196,382-byte request, so describing
twenty rather than fifty takes about a third off the whole thing.

**What it does not say** is whether the model then picks right. This
measures only whether the right tool was in front of it, which is the
half that can be computed. Fewer distractors may help or hurt, and that
wants the tool suite run both ways.

**The four it cannot find are descriptions, not retrieval.** *"who is
the chief minister of Tamil Nadu"* puts `web_search` at #78: nothing in
that tool's own words looks like a general-knowledge question. The same
blindness is what made it answer the Jailer 2 question from memory, so
fixing the description would lift the model's own choosing as well as
the ranking.

The registry the evals build now carries every domain the server has,
including coming, web, maps and calling. Without them the first run
scored a 82% ceiling and reported sixteen misses that were tools never
offered to the ranking at all.

**The tool block does cost time, and I had said it did not** (18
October 2026). The claim that the first word arrives at 2.94s whatever
the prompt carries rested on two calls out of seventy, in a sample
where sixty-eight sat at the same size. `make evals-toolcost` asks the
same one-word question nine times at each size, alternating rather
than in blocks, because the gateway is slower at some minutes than
others:

| tools sent | tool bytes | first word |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 2 | 2.356 s |
| 20 | 48,825 | 2.944 s |
| 50 | 124,501 | 3.657 s |

Roughly in proportion to size, and **about 0.71 s between fifty tools
and twenty**. Five spins was not enough to order them -- twenty came
back slower than fifty, which is the shape of noise -- so the sample is
raised with `EVAL_SPINS`.

**What that makes the tool-retrieval work worth.** Every call in a turn
carries the block, and a turn averaged 2.77 calls on 18 October, so
describing twenty by meaning rather than fifty by a fixed list is worth
about **two seconds off a median turn of 7.1 s**. It also takes about a
third off what every request costs, and raises the odds of the right
tool being in front of the model from 79% to 96%. Those were already
measured; the seconds were the part in doubt, and are not any more.

**The description did not need fixing; the text it is ranked by did**
(18 October 2026, continuing the tool-retrieval measurement).

The plan was to rewrite `web_search`'s description, because it sat at
#78 of 88 for *"who is the chief minister of Tamil Nadu"* and the
description says, in those words, *who holds an office*. It already
said the right thing. It also already carried worked examples --
*"what time does Phoenix Mall close"*, *"is it going to rain
tomorrow"* -- which are two of the questions it was failing.

**It is 3,999 characters, and bge-base reads about 512 tokens.** Its
examples are past the cut and never reach the embedder at all. Seven of
the eighty-eight tools are longer than the embedder reads:
`web_search`, `calendar_events`, `event_recent`, `coming_settled`,
`reminder_set`, `mail_search`, `memory_remember`.

So the fix is to rank on text written to fit, rather than on the whole
of what the model reads. Four ways, over the same 91 cases:

| nearest N | purpose + usewhen + avoid | purpose only | purpose + usewhen | **purpose + the questions it is for** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | 82% | 68% | 76% | **82%** |
| 10 | 91% | 82% | 87% | **92%** |
| 15 | 93% | 85% | 90% | **96%** |
| 20 | 96% | 87% | 91% | **98%** |
| `hot`, today | | | | **79%** |

A tool's `Examples` are questions, and a query is a question, so the
shortest document is also the best one. **Fifteen chosen this way beat
the whole description at twenty, and nothing the model reads changes**
-- which is the part that matters, since a description rewrite would
have had to be measured against tool choice as well.

A guess that was wrong on the way: that the rulebook was burying the
subject, and ranking on `Purpose` alone would do better. It is the
worst of the four. More of a tool's own words helps, right up to the
point where the embedder stops reading.

The two it still cannot find are both about conversations -- *"switch
to the one about cricket"*, *"I've finished with this one"* -- which
name no subject a tool description could match.

**Choosing twenty tools by meaning beats the hand-written list by
fourteen cases** (18 October 2026, the measurement the retrieval work
was for).

The tool suite now runs three ways -- `EVAL_TOOLS=all|hot|nearest`,
with `EVAL_NEAREST` for how many -- so what it measures is what a
request actually carries. Before this it described every tool in full,
which is not what the server sends and never was.

| what is described in full | right first try |
| --- | --- |
| `hot`, the hand-written 25, what the server sends today | **85 of 106** |
| the 20 nearest the question, by meaning | **99 of 106** |

Eighty per cent against ninety-three, on the same 106 questions, with
the same model.

**And neither run asked what a tool is, once.** `tool_describe` was
never the first call in either. When the right tool is a name rather
than a description, the model does not ask -- it reaches for a
different tool and gets it wrong. Deferral has been costing accuracy
and nothing was recovering it, which is the opposite of what the
mechanism was built to do.

On the memory questions alone the gap is starkest: `hot` 3 of 8,
nearest-20 8 of 8. `memory_search` is not in `hot`, so a question about
what he once said arrived with no way to look it up and no sign that
anything was missing.

So all four numbers move the same way at once: **93% against 80% on
reaching the right tool, 0.71s off every model call, about a third off
what a request costs, and 98% against 79% on the right tool being
offered at all.**

**The laptop's tools were never the blocker; a stale comment was** (18
October 2026, asked to *"fix the laptop tools first"*).

Twice today I told the owner that the laptop's twenty-nine tools have
to be described in full because `tool_describe` knows only the server's
own. That was true until 15 October, when `Registry.With` was given a
line that rebuilds `tool_describe` over the copy -- for exactly this
reason, and the comment there says so. The comment at the other end, in
`execute.go`, was left behind, and I read it twice as the state of the
world.

`TestADevicesToolCanBeDescribed` now holds the capability: a registry
with a device's tool added answers `tool_describe` for it.

**What actually stops the twenty-nine being deferred** is the line
beside that comment, `revealed[x.Name] = true`, which marks every one
of them described-already. Removing it is one line, and it should not
be removed on its own. Measured the same day: the model does not call
`tool_describe` when the tool it wants arrives as a name -- across two
full runs of the tool suite it was never the first call -- it reaches
for something else and is wrong. Deferring the laptop's tools with
nothing choosing which to describe would cost the laptop rather than
the bytes.

So the order is the reverse of what it looked like: the picker is not
waiting on the laptop's tools, the laptop's tools are waiting on the
picker.

**One engine, two stores** (owner, 18 October 2026, asked which part of
the embedding should be separate for client and server: *"separate
stores, one engine"*).

The picker is back, with the two things the evening taught, and off by
default.

**Two stores.** The server's own tools are fixed at a build and
embedded once at startup. A device's come and go with the laptop,
arrive per chat, and change whenever the client's own source does.
Mixed into one map a laptop that is away leaves its tools ranked
against questions it cannot answer, and nothing can be cleared without
clearing the lot. `Forget(Device)` drops one side; what it no longer
holds is kept rather than hidden, as everything unranked is.

**What is searched with is the question and the line before it.** Owner,
on "say Deepika's birthday" / "are you sure, sir?" / "yes": *"this yes
separately won't have meaning, then how will embedding give the correct
tool?"* He is right, and measured against the real embedder:

| searched with | calendar_events lands at |
| --- | --- |
| the question itself | #1 |
| a bare "yes", alone | **#75 of 88** |
| "yes" with what was just said | #4 |
| "yes" with both turns | #2 |

Alone it finds `place_near` and `call_offer`. The fix costs nothing --
the same one call over a longer string -- and the line before is
trimmed to 300 characters so a long answer cannot drown the question.
It is the assistant's own last words and not the person's: what the
person said before is usually another subject, while what the assistant
said is what a bare answer is answering.

**And the 94-second turn was not this.** `"platform ai request"` is
logged after `http.Do` returns, not when it is sent, so the gap in the
log is the gateway's: tools chosen at 20:22:27.931, first byte back at
20:23:55. The picker spent 29 ms.

**A tool is ranked on its arguments as well** (18 October 2026, from
guidance the owner brought on how tool retrieval is done elsewhere:
convert name, description *and parameter specifications* into the text
you search).

We were not using the parameters. Measured over the same 91 questions:

| nearest N | without the arguments | with them |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | 82% | **88%** |
| 10 | 92% | **95%** |
| 15 | 96% | **97%** |
| 20 | **98%** | 97% |

One point worse at twenty and six better at five, which is the right
trade: twenty is not where a request gets smaller, ten is.

The owner's own question is the example. Asked *"do I have anything
tomorrow"*, `calendar_events` came **26th of 88** without the arguments
and **15th** with -- inside what gets sent. *"what have I got on
tomorrow"* went 29th to 18th. A tool that takes `from`, `to` and `days`
looks like a question about tomorrow; a sentence about reading
calendars does not.

Each argument contributes its name and sixty characters of what it is
for, sorted -- a map's order is not stable, and a vector that moves
between restarts can be neither cached nor compared.

**What this does not fix.** The scores are still crammed together:
0.093 between the best tool and the twentieth, on a scale where
everything sits near 0.5. `web_search` and `reminder_list` still beat
the diary for a question about the diary. That is the embedding model,
not the text, and `bge-m3` is downloading to find out whether a bigger
one separates them.

**A search is offered whatever the ranking says** (owner, 18 October
2026, told that ten tools carry the right one on 95% of questions
rather than 97%: *"make search tool always inside so even if it misses,
the job is still done."*).

The twentieth question is the one this is for. A ranking that misses
leaves the model with nothing that fits and no way to ask: measured the
same day, it does not call `tool_describe` when the tool it wants is
only a name -- it reaches for something else and is wrong. With a
search in the list it can at least go and look.

`web_search` alone. It is the one that answers a question about
anything rather than about one thing, so it is the only one whose
absence leaves nothing to fall back on; adding the others would be
adding them to every question, which is the fixed list this replaced.

Beside the nearest and not instead of one of them, so asking for ten
still ranks ten deep.

**Tavily behind web_search** (owner, 18 October 2026, after looking at
the free search services and the MCP servers that wrap them: *"yes add
tavily behind web_search."*).

Not an MCP server, and that was the thing worth settling first. MCP is
a way to call a search, not a way to get one free; it would have added
a process, a hop and nine tools to a registry we spent the evening
cutting to thirteen, and brought its own tool description after a day
spent measuring how much descriptions matter.

**The deciding number was his own usage.** Thirty-three web searches in
the whole history of this server, two to four on a busy day -- about
ninety a month against Tavily's thousand free credits. Quota is not a
constraint for this person and neither is price, so the only questions
left were quality, speed and where the questions go.

**Three services, two Pairs.** A `search.Pair` is itself a
`search.Service`, so TinyFish stays in front and behind it sits Tavily
then Firecrawl. Tavily before Firecrawl because Firecrawl's five
hundred a month is the scarcer allowance of the two that count.

What Tavily returns is cleaned page text rather than a list of links,
which is what a model about to answer actually wants. A basic search is
asked for explicitly: it costs one credit, and their `auto_parameters`
costs two because it may choose the dearer depth for you.

**Two things their API does differently.** It has no "last N days" --
`Ask.Days` becomes a `start_date`, because "the last three days" is
what was asked and "the last week" is not. And `/extract` answers 200
with everything in `failed_results` when nothing could be fetched, so
both arrays are read: a reader handed an empty list and no error would
say the pages were blank rather than that they could not be had.

**432 and 429 are told apart from a fault**, and become
`search.ErrSpent`, which is what makes the Pair rest a service rather
than ask it again.

`isNil` is there because a `*tavily.Client` that is nil is not an
untyped nil: inside a Pair it would satisfy the interface and fail on
every call.

Off until a key is set. `[search] tavily_key` is in `config.ini`,
commented. `config.example.ini` has no `[search]` section at all, which
predates this.

**Tavily is not the best, so it stays the fallback** (owner, having
added the key: *"use tavily if its the best."* It is not).

`make evals-searching` asks all three the same five real questions --
the two that were answered from memory this morning, two about now, and
one about a place -- and prints what each came back with.

| | median | worst | failed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| firecrawl | **936 ms** | 1.59 s | 0 |
| tinyfish | 1.51 s | 3.26 s | 0 |
| tavily | **2.49 s** | 3.09 s | 0 |

**It is the slowest of the three, by a wide margin**, and its answers
are not better for it. Asked for tomorrow's weather it returned a raw
JSON blob -- `{'location': {'name': 'Chennai', 'region': …` -- as its
first result and a Delhi forecast as its second, where the other two
gave readable Chennai forecasts. Asked the mall's hours it gave
"Standard operating hours are d…" where both others surfaced "Mall
timings: 10:00 AM - 10:00 PM" verbatim.

All three got the chief minister right, which was the question that
started this.

So nothing is promoted. The order stands: TinyFish first because it is
quick enough and has no allowance at all; Tavily behind it as a free,
independent fallback; Firecrawl last because its five hundred a month
is the scarcest thing in the chain -- though it is, on this showing,
the fastest of the three, which is worth remembering if the order is
ever revisited.

Five questions and one run, so the snippet problems are the finding and
the milliseconds are an impression. The gap is wide enough to act on
either way.

**Deep search is a parameter, not a job** (owner, 18 October 2026, on
what deep research should be here: *"I want deep research in the chat
call only, coz I'll ask to cross-check and research there .. so just
add a parameter deep research in web_search."*).

`web_search` takes `deep`. With it, the tool searches, then reads the
top three pages in one batch, and hands the model the results and the
pages' own words together, under a line telling it to compare them and
say where they disagree.

**One tool call and not a conversation**, which is what makes it fit a
turn at all. The turn is cut at thirty seconds and a round of the model
costs four and a half, so rounds are the thing that cannot be afforded;
reading is one more HTTP call on a service that takes every URL at
once. An agent that searched, thought, searched again would be minutes
and belongs in a background pass -- which is what was offered and what
he turned down.

What it buys is the only cross-checking worth the name: three sources'
own words side by side, rather than one summary and the model's memory
of the rest.

A read that fails does not fail the search. The results still stand and
a thinner answer beats a refusal.

Rejected on the way: Tavily's `/research` endpoint, which is the same
idea bought rather than built. It is queued and takes minutes, so it
cannot live in a turn; it costs 4 to 110 credits a time against a
thousand a month; and it cannot see his diary, his memories or his
devices, which is the one thing a research agent here can do that no
vendor's can.

**The battery rate is worked out here, not in the model's head**
(owner, 18 October 2026, shown an answer of twelve hours to a charge
that took forty-five minutes: *"its wrong."*).

Two faults in one answer, and both are the same mistake.

**It measured the wrong window.** It asked for two readings --
`{"kind":"battery.level","limit":2}` -- and got 23% at 22:35 and 24% at
22:47. The phone was plugged in at **22:46**. Eleven of those twelve
minutes were it draining, so what it measured was the discharge rate.
The true rate, from the readings either side, was **one percent every
thirty-five seconds**: about forty-five minutes to full.

**And the arithmetic was wrong anyway.** On its own figure of twelve
minutes a percent with 76% to go, that is 912 minutes -- **15.2 hours**
-- and it said twelve.

So `events.Moving` does it. Asked anything about `battery.level`,
`event_recent` now appends a finished sentence: which way it is going,
how long a percent takes, and how long to full or empty. Twelve
readings whatever the caller asked for, only those since the last plug
or unplug, and only those a minute past it -- a phone jumps a percent
or two the moment it is connected, and that jump is not a rate.

Nothing is said when it cannot be said honestly: fewer than two
readings since the state changed, or no movement between them. The
model still has the readings and can describe what it sees.

This is [[a-span-is-said-not-counted]] again, in a second place. Handed
two figures and a subtraction, a model does the subtraction in its head
and gets it wrong. `events.Span` renders a duration the way somebody
says it -- "45 minutes", "2 hours", "15.2 hours" -- so the division
never reaches the model at all.

**A described tool expires** (owner, 18 October 2026: *"do that, expire
a described tool after a few turns."*).

He asked about his battery, then about a film, then about two people,
then said **"look again"**. It read his battery.

The battery tool had been described three questions earlier, and
`alreadyDescribed` walked the whole window: anything ever called or
described in it stayed described. So a bare follow-up went looking for
something to look at again and found a tool nobody had mentioned since.

The ranking was not at fault and the picker was not at fault. With the
previous answer attached, `web_search` ranked **2nd of 88** and
`event_recent` **13th** -- outside the ten it would have been given. It
was offered anyway, as a leftover.

Now only the last **three** of his turns count, by chat rather than by
message: one thing he says is one chat however many rounds it takes,
and a turn that called four tools must not push the turn before it out
of sight. A chain -- ask, refine, correct -- keeps its tools. Another
subject's do not.

Messages written before chats were recorded have no chat of their own
and are kept, since an old message cannot be placed and dropping what
cannot be placed would quietly shrink the window on the oldest
conversations.

**Also that evening, and not fixed by this.** Asked whether two people
were going to marry, it answered that nothing had been announced --
twice, with `web_search` ranked first of eighty-eight and offered both
times, and after the send-back told it to look. `lookFirst` now bans
the sentences rather than stating the rule: that nothing has been
announced, that there is no public word, that it has not happened, has
not been released, is not known. That is the form that worked for the
word "tool" in `persona.machinery`.

Unmeasured, and the eval says so: both test questions reach
`web_search` in the harness with and without the change, so the harness
does not reproduce what a real turn does. The rule is reasoned, not
proven -- the third time today that a carried-subject or look-first
rule has been broken while present and correct in the prompt.

**A deeper search is its own decision** (owner, 18 October 2026, shown
*"I can search more deeply if you would like, sir"*: *"it's asking for
a permission to do deep research — don't need to ask that, it can do it
on its own."*).

The fault was mine and it was a contradiction, not a rule being
ignored. `replying` has forbidden ending on an offer of further help
since it was written. But the `deep` parameter, added two hours
earlier, described itself as *"for when they ask you to cross-check,
to look into something properly, to be sure"* -- which is an
instruction to wait and be asked.

So the description said offer and the persona said never offer, and the
description won, because it is the one sitting beside the tool at the
moment of choosing.

Now: set it yourself the moment a plain search has not answered -- a
summary that stops short, results about the wrong thing, a detail the
snippets do not carry -- and never offer and wait. `keepLooking` says
the same from the other end: searching deeper is part of not giving up,
beside searching again with different words, and giving up now takes
both having failed.

The lesson is not that the model broke a rule. Two instructions
disagreed and the nearer one was obeyed, which is what should happen.
Every rule written beside a tool is read against the persona, and a new
parameter is a new chance to contradict it.

**The gateway will not let a round be told it must call a tool** (18
October 2026, the question asked twice and finally answered).

Five times that day the round after a send-back was told to use a tool,
had the right one ranked first and offered, and answered from memory
anyway: the terminal, the marriage question, "look again", and both
halves of the earbuds exchange. The instruction is advice and the model
declines it, so the only thing that would make it a rule is
`tool_choice`.

`make evals-mustcall` asks the gateway directly. Every form is refused:

| sent | answer |
| --- | --- |
| nothing | called `calendar_events` |
| `"auto"`, `"required"` | **Invalid JSON format in request body** |
| `{"type":"any"}`, `{"type":"auto"}` | **Unexpected key found in request body** |
| `{"type":"tool","name":…}` | **Unexpected key** |
| `{"type":"function","function":{…}}` | **Unexpected key** |

So the door is shut. There is no way through this gateway to require a
tool call, and the field is kept only so that the next person does not
spend an evening rediscovering it -- `environment.Request.MustUseTool`
is never set, and `omitempty` keeps it off the wire.

**What that means for this class of fault.** At the model layer, words
are all there is. The remaining levers are all on our side of the call:
what is offered (the picker), what has expired (`Lately`), what the
tool itself does before the model sees it (`events.Moving`,
`compared`), and what the server refuses to send afterwards
(`tool.Unchanged`). Those have worked every time this evening. The
rules written into prompts have failed five times.

That is the thing to remember the next time something is answered
wrongly: ask what the server can decide, before writing another
sentence for the model to weigh.

**An answer that is only a question is sent back with its subject**
(owner, 18 October 2026, shown *"A deep research into what, sir?"*
after a whole exchange about a pair of earbuds).

It asked twice -- the second time after the send-back had already told
it to look. `carried` says, in those words, *never ask which of them
they meant when your own last answer says which*. The gateway will not
let a round be required to call a tool. So neither the rule nor the
provider can stop it.

What the server can do is stop asking the model to work out the subject
and hand it over. It has the previous answer; that is the subject.

**Detected by punctuation and length, not by words.** An answer ending
in a question mark, one sentence long, from a turn that touched no
tool. `replying` allows three questions at the end of an answer and all
three follow having looked at something -- which of several things a
tool returned, whether to make what was not there, whether to write
down what was arranged -- so a turn that used no tool catches none of
them. Once per turn, or an obstinate round is a loop somebody waits
through.

**And it found a second fault while being built.** `lastSaid` took the
newest assistant message of any kind, and naming a conversation is
written as one: the first draft of the subject prompt handed over *"I
have called this conversation an answer."* It now takes only
`conversation.Chat`. The same function feeds the tool picker's search
text, so that was being polluted too.

**web_search had nothing in it about a thing you could buy** (18
October 2026, the last of the four faults in the earbuds exchange).

Asked *"what about the microphone settings?"* after an answer about a
pair of earbuds, it read the laptop's own settings. The reason was
vocabulary, laid out plainly once the three ranking texts are side by
side:

    choose_device   "Choose the microphone or speaker … earbuds when they are connected"
    get_settings    "This app's settings … the wake word …"
    web_search      "who won the match last night. what time does Phoenix Mall close.
                     is it going to rain tomorrow. what is trending on Tamil social media"

`choose_device` owned both of his words. `web_search` owned neither,
because every example it carried was a result, a mall, the weather or a
trend. **Nothing in it was about a product.**

Three examples added -- a product's specifications, its battery and
noise cancellation, which phone to buy -- and the purpose widened from
"anything that is not about them" to name what it covers: what a thing
is and what it costs, a product and its specifications, a place, a
person, a result, the news.

| question | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "microphone settings", with the earbuds answer before it | #26 | **#1** |
| "I was asking about realme earbuds" | #16 | **#1** |
| "microphone settings" alone, with no context | #47 | #11 |

And no over-reach: over the suite the right tool is in the nearest ten
on **94%** against 92% before, and in the nearest twenty on 98%.

The lesson is the one that keeps paying. A tool is found by the words
in its own description, and the words it lacks are the questions it
will never be offered for. Every example is a shape it can be found
by; a tool with four examples can be found four ways.

**The question guard asked for one sentence and they come in two** (19
October 2026, the same fault twice in one exchange: *"why is it not
getting the context???"*).

```
I need to know what you are asking about, sir. Your decision on what?
I need to know what you want me to search for, sir. Search for anything about what?
```

Both reached him. The send-back fired on both, and `onlyAsking`
required `Sentences(answer) <= 1` -- so a question split across two
sentences walked past a guard written the night before for exactly
this.

Counted in characters now, not sentences. The two that escaped were 69
and 83; `Asked` is 200, and an answer carrying something real and then
asking runs well past it.

The test that was supposed to hold the other side -- an answer that
says something and then asks -- was also wrong, and in a way that hid
this. It used *"There is no list called that, sir. Shall I make one?"*
with no tool call, which cannot happen: to know the list is not there
it must have looked. Written faithfully, with a tool and a real
sentence in front of the question, it passes either way and stops
arguing for a narrow rule.

**Every tool the picker chose was being refused** (19 October 2026,
and mine, from the evening before).

Asked to open Places, it answered: *"I asked to open Places but the
tool was not run because I had not been given its arguments. I cannot
open Places without them."* Three things wrong in one answer, and one
cause.

`go_to` ranked **third of eighty-eight** for that question and was
described. The model called it. The server refused it.

`Registry.Withheld` asked whether a tool was **hot or revealed**. While
those two decided what went out, that was the same question as "was it
described". Since the picker was switched on it is a different
question, and the two answers came apart: a tool the picker chose and
sent is not hot and nothing revealed it, so **every non-hot tool the
picker offered was refused the moment it was called.**

`place_visits` is in the hot list, so the second half of his question
worked and hid the first.

`Registry.Undescribed` asks what this request actually described, and
the runner now computes that set in `offered` -- the only place that
knows, since a picker chooses it per question and asking the registry
again answers for a different request. `Withheld` remains, as
`Undescribed` over hot plus revealed, which is what it always meant.

The two other faults in that answer follow from this one and need no
fix of their own: the machinery leak was it reading out the refusal,
and `tool.Unchanged` was right that a change had been asked for and
had not happened.

The lesson for the picker: switching on a new way of choosing what
goes out means auditing everything that asks *what went out*. I
changed the first and not the second, and it was silently wrong from
that evening until this morning.

**"Okay" to an offer was a shrug** (19 October 2026).

A terminal reaction announced *"Claude Code in Server has finished the
GLiNER run, sir -- shall I ask it to say the numbers?"*. He answered
*"Okay."* and got *"Very well, sir."* -- eight tokens, no tool, nothing
done.

Nothing was missing. His laptop had offered twenty-eight tools,
`type_into_terminal` among them; ninety-four were reachable and twelve
were described. The turn simply never went back to look:

    execute.go  "said in passing: not sent back to look"

`okay` and `ok` are on the in-passing list, whose own comment reads
*"Never a yes: a yes to something offered is answered by doing it."*
The principle was written down and then contradicted two lines later,
because "okay" alone really is a shrug. What tells the two apart is not
the word but what came before it.

`InPassing` now takes the assistant's own last words. When those ended
in a question, `okay`, `ok`, `okay then`, `alright`, `all right` and
`fine` are an instruction and go back to look. Only those: an
acknowledgement -- got it, understood, cool -- is not consent even
after a question, and a refusal is not either.

The question is found by `lastAloud`, which is wider than `lastSaid`.
An offer can come from an announcement as easily as from a reply --
this one was `conversation.Immediate` -- so it was never in the reply
history at all. `Renaming` is skipped there for the reason `lastSaid`
skips it: it counts as an announcement, never ends in a question, and
would hide the question before it.

The lesson: a guard that reads one turn in isolation cannot tell a
shrug from a yes. The ambiguity is between turns, so the guard has to
see the turn before.

**What a question names, and where each name belongs** (19 October 2026).

The plan is that only the persona goes to the model every time, and what
the question is about is looked up and injected. That needs the names out
of the sentence first, and no model tested could find them. Measured over
140 of his own questions:

| | all 140 | the 22 carrying a time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| answer "none" always | 84% | 0 of 22 |
| qwen2.5:1.5b, free | 45% | -- |
| qwen2.5:1.5b, forced | 11% | -- |
| bge-base nearest prototype | 89% | 10 of 22 |
| GLiNER small-v2.1 | 90% | 14 of 22 |
| a word list | 100% | 22 of 22 |

Two of those were my own fault rather than the model's. qwen was allowed
to write free text, so 47 answers were off the list -- which is a missing
schema, not a misunderstanding. Then it was forced to choose, on a job
where 118 of 140 questions have no time in them at all, with no way to
say none.

**Dates are a word list, not a model.** Stripped of the one phrase fitted
to the data -- "right now" -- it still scores 96% and 17 of 22, on
nothing but month names, weekday names, tomorrow, yesterday, today and
tonight.

**Names are GLiNER**, which is not a writing model: it is given the
labels at call time and answers spans cut out of the sentence, so a name
it reports was certainly said. 47ms median on CPU, 60ms through the Go
client, 59ms slowest over thirty real questions. The weights are 610MB
and fetched once.

**Three answers, not one.** Over 91 spans from those questions:

- the word lists keep every span worth a lookup and four that are not --
  100% recall, 84% precision. Recall is what matters: a name wrongly
  dropped is a lookup that never happens, and a name wrongly kept is one
  query that finds nothing.
- looking a name up in what the server already holds is never wrong and
  finds 9 of 22. Alone it is useless as a filter.

So the lookup does not filter, it **sorts**. A name the record holds is
his and is asked of his own record, spelt the way the record spells it. A
name it does not hold is real but worldly -- Spotify, Chennai, Coolie --
and his own record cannot answer for it. Everything else is not a name.
That middle answer is what neither half could give alone.

Three sources feed the record, all already kept: the nightly list of
names he says, the places he has drawn, and the names his own devices
reported. The last are worth most, for the reason `vocabulary/heard.go`
already gives -- a contact name read off the phone is spelt the way he
spells it, and the same name through a microphone is a guess.

**`heard.Best` matched "Tada" to "Alekhya Chintada".** Found by running
thirty of his real questions through the whole chain: *"Search online
about Alekhya in Tada"* sent a town to his contacts. `heard.Normalise`
strips the spaces, so the containment rule that matches "holidays" to
"Holidays in India" is a bare substring test by the time it runs, and
"tada" is inside "alekhyachintada". Four characters clears `Shortest`.

Left alone where it is: five tools match titles with it, and loosening
or tightening that is its own decision. `pointing` matches strictly
instead -- exact, or one name beginning another, or likeness -- which
keeps "realme" for "realme Buds Air8" and refuses Tada.

Likeness earns its place elsewhere in the same set: "Jaylen" in *"Is
Jaylen will be releasing tomorrow?"* is "Jailer" misheard, and the record
holds Jailer because he talks about the film. It scores 0.667 against a
bar of 0.6 and nothing else comes near -- Spotify to Spectra is 0.286,
Chennai to Chintada 0.500.

**Nothing uses it yet.** It runs beside every turn and writes down what
it would have looked up, so it can be read against real questions before
it changes an answer. What each route should prefetch is the next
decision. `make evals-pointing` holds the numbers; the service is
`deployments/gliner-service.py` behind `[naming]` in the config, on 8092
because `tei-m3` still holds 8091 from the rejected bge-m3 trial.

**The conversation in front of you comes first** (19 October 2026).

Owner, on being told a sleep note from four days ago had answered a
question about the sentence directly above it: *"the first priority is
the current conversation!!"*

`memory.precedence` is the ladder every recalled line is read against,
and it names only one rung above them -- a tool that can answer now. The
conversation in progress is not on it at all. It is first.

The fault it cost. He asked *"Why did you say that?"* about *"Dr.Yenyen
is a PlayStation jailbreak developer on X, sir"*, and was told *"I said
that because you have a note asking me to advise you to sleep if you are
still talking after 2 AM, sir."* That sentence was in the prompt, as a
recalled exchange from 15 October scoring 0.712, and it was reused almost
word for word.

All three exchanges recalled for that turn were other times he had said
"why did you say that". Searching by meaning matched the **wording of the
question**, because a question with no subject in it has nothing else to
match on. The subject was in the line above, and the line above was not
part of the search.

**The obvious fix is wrong, and I nearly shipped it.** The tool picker
had what looked like the same bug and was fixed on 18 October -- "yes"
alone put the diary 75th of 88 tools and 4th with the line before it --
so the same was built here: search the memory and the transcript with the
question and the line before it. On this one turn it works, and the sleep
exchange does not come back at all.

Over 107 real turns it is worse. Judged by whether the nearest exchange
shares a content word with what was asked, a measure that is not my eye:

| searched with | shares a word with the question |
| --- | --- |
| the question alone | 85/107, 79% |
| the question and the line before | 53/107, 50% |

The line before is usually the assistant's own answer about something
else, and at up to 300 characters it swamps a five-word question. The
picker wants the conversation's subject and this wants *this question's*
subject, which is not the same want. Reverted, and `conversation.Latest`
with it.

**What was shipped instead.** The harmful exchange was the **third of
three**, at 0.712 under a top of 0.818; the first two were both the
assistant saying it could not tell what "that" meant, which is harmless.
So `MaxQuoted` is 1. At one it never arrives.

With it, `Least = 0.55`: a search always returns its nearest however far
away that is, and over 1146 turns the best match averaged 0.655 and went
as low as 0.378, with every one of them going into the prompt. "Yes, do
it." matched "yes" at 0.603. "You can use step search" matched an old "I
have no tool for that" at 0.600 -- the stale-refusal trap, fed in.

The floor is deliberately low, because the noise reaches 0.70 and no line
separates it cleanly. Raising it is a measurement, not an argument.

`Quoted` already warns the model about exactly this -- *"chosen for
resembling the question, which is not the same as bearing on it, so
ignoring all of them is often right"* -- and the warning was in the
running binary when it happened. A rule the model has to weigh loses,
again. So `memory.precedence` now names the conversation as the first
rung, which is correct and is not what is relied on: the count and the
floor are.

**Four hours against a true fifty minutes** (19 October 2026).

Asked *"my phone is in charging how long it will take to charge full"*,
it answered *"it charged from nine percent to fourteen percent at
fourteen forty-five... At that rate it will take roughly four hours."*
The phone had been plugged in **23 seconds earlier** and was climbing at
35 seconds a percent -- 13% at 16:43:46, 17% at 16:46:07 -- so the
answer was about fifty minutes.

The rate was never handed to it. The model called:

    event_recent {"kind": "power.charging", "limit": 1}

which is a fair way to ask, and `asksBattery` matched only
`battery.level`, `battery` and `battery.`. So `Moving` never ran. The
one event that came back has the value `unknown`, because the phone
cannot report charging state at all -- see
[[charging-state-comes-from-home-assistant]] -- and with no rate in
front of it the model did the arithmetic itself, across an unplug an
hour earlier, mixing two charging sessions.

That is word for word what `Moving`'s own comment says will happen:
*handed two figures and a subtraction, a model does the subtraction in
its head and gets it wrong.* The guard was right and was never reached.

`asksBattery` now matches both families, `battery.` and `power.`, with
or without the dot.

**The half that matters is the empty answer.** The rate was computed
only after the early return for a window that held nothing, and
`power.charging` is exactly the kind that finds nothing -- it is stale,
and its value never varies. So the case that caused this was the one
case the rate could not reach. It is now attached to `Nothing` as well
as to `describe`.

The lesson, and it is the second time today: when a guard exists and the
fault happens anyway, check whether the guard ran before changing what
it says. Both faults today were a correct guard that nothing reached.

**The instruction read back as a promise** (19 October 2026).

Jarvis offered to tell Claude Code to carry on. He said *"ok"*. It
answered:

> Understood, sir. I will search before claiming that anything has not
> happened, does not exist, or is unknown. I will read both lists of
> tools before saying I cannot do something. If a tool fits, I will use
> it.

That is `lookFirst`, read back to him almost word for word. Three
guards were involved and all three behaved as written.

The *"okay" after a question* fix held: the turn was not said in
passing, and it did go back to look. Its first answer was one word,
`Sir.`, which the send-back then discarded.

**Why it answered the instruction.** Every send-back appended only a
user turn -- the question, then the instruction, with nothing between
them. The model never saw its own answer, so `lookFirst` arrived as the
person speaking and it replied to the person. The same gap is why *"say
it shorter"* produces a fresh answer rather than a shorter one, which is
the likeliest reason a send-back improves an answer about as often as it
spoils it: 8 better, 5 worse, 12 the same, over the 25 cases that carry
their draft.

`asAnswer` now puts the answer into the history before the instruction,
at all five send-backs.

**It cannot reach the one that caused this.** `lookFirst` is begun
