speculatively, while the first answer is still being written -- which is
the only reason a needless send-back costs 0.11s instead of a round. A
request sent before the answer existed cannot carry it, and the code
already said so about `alsoShorter`: *"It cannot reach a round that was
already running when the send-back was decided."* In this log that is
**109 send-backs of 109**. So the change is live for the other four --
say it shorter, say it plainly, finish it, the subject is -- which are
the instructions actually about the text, and dead for look-first.

Closing that needs the speculation given up on look-first: a full round,
roughly four seconds, on the 17% of turns that send back. Not taken
here; it is a trade for the owner to make, and `make evals-doubting`
holds the 179 cases to measure it against.

**Two other faults in the same answer, both still open.** It said
"tools" twice and `persona.NamesMachinery` did not fire. And
`type_into_terminal` was among the 41 tools described to it that turn,
so telling Claude Code to carry on was reachable and it never tried.

## A second prompt, written rather than condensed

The persona that runs is configuration: `[assistant] persona`, `jarvis`
or `jarvis-brief`, with both compiled in and nothing deleted either
way. `jarvis` is 28,914 characters. `jarvis-brief` is about 4,000.

The owner asked for the short one on 19 October 2026 -- *"i think we
should condense the system prompt .. have it as a developmental flag
.. so both sys prompts exist, let's try with the condensed one and if
it doesn't work we will revert back"*. It is an experiment with a
switch, not a replacement.

### Why a long prompt gets long

Thirteen rules in `jarvis` were added after something went wrong, and
each one is a sentence about that thing. They accumulate because
nothing ever removes them: the incident is over, the sentence stays,
and the next incident adds another. By the end the document is
organised by its own history instead of by its subject, and the model
reads three sentences about hand-backs in three different places.

What made the short one possible is that the rules that actually hold
are not in either prompt. A wall of prose, a buried date, a hand-back,
the word "tool", a reply that is only a question, a change claimed and
not made: each is checked in `internal/domain/persona` after the
answer is written, and none of it depends on prompt wording. Thirteen
prompt rules lost in a single day's traffic. Everything that held was
a count or a check.

### The patch that proved the point

The first `jarvis-brief` was a condensation, and within the hour it
had a patch bolted on: three sentences listing phrases it may not
send, added after it told the owner there was no news of a film
without searching. That is the same habit, on a document a day old.

So it was rewritten the same evening -- *"the new v2 prompt should not
cover the patches, it should have a proper prompt"* -- organised by
subject, with every rule stated once where it belongs:

| Section | What it is about |
| --- | --- |
| `briefManner` | bearing, and nothing else |
| `briefAnswering` | what they want, and how a reply ends |
| `briefKnowing` | what it can know, and what it must look up |
| `briefSpoken` / `briefWritten` | the same answer, heard or skimmed |
| `briefHonesty` | the line it does not cross |

The banned sentences survive, but not as a list of phrases appended to
the end. They are the consequence of the paragraph above them: two
things are never in you and always a call away, their own life and the
world since training, so there is no such thing as not knowing, only
not having looked -- *therefore* these sentences may not be sent
without searching first. A rule that follows from something is one the
model can apply to a case the rule never named.

**The decision is general.** A rule goes in the section it is about,
derived from what that section is for. Where it exists because
something went wrong, the rule goes in the prompt and the incident
goes in the commit. If a fix will not fit that way, that is the sign
it belongs in a check and not in prose at all.

### What holds it

`make evals-diary` 7/7 and `make evals-looking` 5/5, on the brief
persona: a date question does not open the diary, and a question about
a credit card, a two-factor setting or a product's battery life is
searched rather than handed back. Four tests in the package hold the
sentences the shape checks depend on. The long prompt is one line of
configuration away for as long as both are compiled in.

## An identifier comes from a listing, on a read as much as a write

He asked *"did I get any mail today?"*, was given ten lines including
*"Netflix -- New film added to your list at 18:00"*, and asked *"whats
the new film?"*. The answer was about Netflix's October releases in
general, ending *"Without the exact message timestamp, I cannot say
which specific one Netflix..."*.

The log says what happened, and it is not what the answer suggests:

```
22:26:14  mail_read {"id": "netflix_new_film"}
22:26:18  web_search {"query": "Netflix new films October 2026"}
          saying="I don't have the message identifier from the l..."
```

It reasoned correctly. It went to his mail first, and it wanted the one
message. It had no identifier, so it made one up in the shape of the
subject line, and when that failed it left the domain it was in and
asked the web instead.

### Why it had no identifier

Deliberately. `conversation.withdrawn` takes the contents out of every
tool result from an earlier turn, identifiers included, because a
result is true when it runs and not afterwards -- four questions in a
row once produced no tool calls at all, every answer coming from
results already in the window, and an event was cancelled by an
identifier from a stale listing. What is left says the tool ran and to
call it again.

That decision is right and stands. The listing it needed was one call
away. It invented an identifier instead.

### Why nothing stopped it

The guard for exactly this exists, and had since September: a call is
refused until its own domain has been listed in the same turn, and the
server does the listing while refusing so the turn does not lose a
round. Its first line was `if !t.Writes`.

`mail_read` is the only tool in the server that requires an identifier
and changes nothing. Every other one -- `calendar_update`,
`reminder_update`, `task_update`, `rule_update`, `rule_quiet`,
`rule_cancel` -- writes, and was covered. The one read fell through the
one condition.

Its own description forbids the mistake twice: *"Needs the identifier
from a listing"*, and *"Do not guess an identifier. It comes from a
listing and nowhere else, and an invented one fails."* The model
guessed anyway. A rule in prose loses; this is the thirteenth time that
has been written down here.

**A failed read is not the smaller harm.** A refused write says so and
stops. A failed read leaves the model holding a question it cannot
answer from the domain it is in, and it goes somewhere else for an
answer rather than looking again. That is how a question about his
inbox became a web search.

### What changed

The guard now asks what it was always about. `beforewriting.go` is
`listfirst.go`, `readFirst` is `listFirst`, and the condition is
`t.Writes || NamesSomething(t)`.

`NamesSomething` is read off the schema -- a required argument named
`id` or `ids`, or an array or object of them -- and not declared on the
tool. A flag is a thing somebody forgets to set on the one tool that
needed it, which is the whole of this fault in a sentence. An optional
identifier does not count: that is a listing narrowed, which is where
identifiers come from.

A refused read no longer opens with "Nothing has been changed", which
on a read is noise about a danger that was never there, and invites the
model to tell him nothing was changed when he asked to be told
something.

### The next one of these

`NewRegistry` now refuses to build a registry in which something takes
an identifier and nothing in its domain lists. It runs at startup, so
it is a server that will not boot rather than an answer that is wrong,
and it needs nobody to remember to run it.

`make test` covers the behaviour: an invented identifier on a read is
refused, the listing is done for it, the same call goes through once it
has run, and the refusal does not talk about changes.

### What was not done

No sentence was added to the prompt. He described the behaviour he
wants -- *"it should first look at the previous message, mostly my
question will be related to that; if not, behave normally"* -- and the
model already did that part: it went to mail, not to the web, and only
fell out of the domain when the call failed. Adding a rule about it
would be a sentence covering a case the code now covers, which is the
habit that made the first prompt 28,914 characters.

### The folded clock was reverted the same night

It went out at 23:10 and broke the first real question he asked:

> **What's the status of the terminal Jarvis Server?**
>
> I understand, sir. I will use 11:24 pm Monday 19 October as the only
> time I have now, never earlier times from this conversation, and keep
> my answers short without losing the fact.

The log shows it did the work. `read_terminal` ran, returned, and the
answer was thrown away for an acknowledgement of the clock.

**The round after a tool is not the round before it.** `execute.go`
sets `prompt = ""` once tools have run, because the question is
already in the history and asking it twice has the model answer it
twice. So on that round there was no question to fold the clock into,
and the branch written for that case sent it as a user message of its
own, standing after the tool results -- which is the exact arrangement
the whole change existed to abolish, reintroduced in the one place the
measurement never looked.

The comment on that branch said *"nothing of the person's stands
beside it there"*. True, and beside the point: nothing had to stand
beside it for the model to answer it.

**What the measurement missed.** Four of four on stale times, none of
eleven follow-ups, none of six plain questions -- and broken on the
first question he asked. The eval asks one round and never runs a
tool, so it never reached the round after one. Roughly half the rounds
that happen are rounds it cannot see.

Reverted to the pair, which has a known and smaller fault: two to six
of eleven subjectless follow-ups answer the clock, and no question
with a subject of its own does.

Three repairs are now measured and none has shipped: a terse receipt
(does not work -- any reply is something the model can see itself
having said), no reply at all (works, but puts two of his turns side
by side), and folding (works on first rounds, breaks continuations).
The pair stands until something beats it on both counts, and the next
attempt is not worth making until the eval runs a tool.

## A yes was answered by reading, not by doing

It offered *"Shall I tell it to keep going?"*, he said **yes**, and the
turn called `read_terminal` twice and gave him the status. The first
draft was *"Yes, sir."*

```
23:33:04  thrown_away="Yes, sir."                     → sent back to look at the tools
23:33:04  thrown_away="I'm not certain what you meant" → sent back with its subject
23:33:08  read_terminal {"terminal": "Jarvis Server"}
23:33:11  read_terminal {"terminal": "Jarvis Server"}
23:33:19  "Jarvis Server is running. Clock bug fixed." …
```

### Everything built for this already ran

- `persona.Agrees("yes")` -- **true**, checked against the real text.
- `persona.Asks(offer)` -- **true**.
- `conversation.SayingYesTo` put the offer in front of the model with
  *"Do what it offered, now, with the terminal or the thing it names --
  not whatever is in front of them."*
- The look-first send-back fired, and the model went and looked.

Nothing was missing from the prompt. The offer was quoted to it, the
instruction was explicit, and it read the terminal instead. That is the
fourteenth rule in this file to lose while sitting in the running
binary.

**What was missing was anything that could tell looking from doing.**
The look-first guard asks whether a tool ran. A read is a tool.

### The count behind the note

`writing.tried` already counts calls to anything that creates, changes
or removes. So the check is one line of state: he agreed to an offer,
and the turn is ending with `tried == 0`. Sent back once, with the
offer restated -- the offer is the instruction, because the model wrote
it and it says exactly what was meant to happen -- and with the thing
that was actually missed said plainly: *reading something is not doing
it, and telling them the state of the thing is not doing it either.*

### Why it is safe to fire on every such turn

An offer can be of words alone. *"Shall I read the numbers out?"* is
one, and a model held to a tool it does not need would invent one. So
the way out is written into the send-back: *"If what you offered was
only to say something, say it again and it will be sent as it is."*
That is how every other send-back here ends, and it means a word-only
offer costs a round and never the answer.

A round is about four seconds of a thirty-second turn. The standing
trade is accuracy over latency, and this is the trade it was written
for.

### What it does not fix

It should not have asked. *"Never end a reply with a question or an
offer of further help"* is in the persona and is enforced nowhere:
`persona.Asks` exists and is used only to work out what a yes means,
never to stop the question being asked. Had the rule held, it would
have said what it was about to do and done it, and there would have
been no yes to mishandle.

That guard is not written here. `onlyAsking` covers an answer that is
nothing but a question, and the hard part of the general case is that
an honest question after a listing -- *"the diary has two of these,
did you mean the Tuesday one?"* -- is wanted, and reads the same way.

### And now it does not ask

The open half of the entry above is closed. *"Never end a reply with a
question or an offer of further help. Where you would ask permission,
say what you are about to do instead"* now has a count behind it:
`persona.Offers` on the answer, `writing.tried == 0`, sent back once.

**The hard part was never detecting a question.** It was telling an
offer from the question the persona wants. `persona.Asks` is a `?` at
the end, and that catches both:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| offer | *"Seven of them, sir. Do you want me to cancel the Tuesday one?"* |
| question | *"The diary has two of these, sir. Did you mean the Tuesday one?"* |

The line is drawn on what the last sentence is **about**: offering to
act, against asking what they meant. First person and the assistant's
own next action -- shall I, should I, would you like me to, do you want
me to, want me to, anything else, let me know if.

`may I` and `can I` are left out on purpose, and so is a bare `would
you like`. Each introduces a clarifier as readily as an offer -- *"can
I confirm which one you meant"* -- and a guard that fires on an honest
question is worse than one that misses an offer, because a missed offer
is caught again the moment he says yes to it.

**What a sentence cannot say** is whether the thing offered can be
undone, and that is the one case the persona does want asked about. So
the send-back names it rather than detecting it: *"Only one thing is
worth asking about first: something that cannot be taken back once it
is done. If that is what this is, ask it as one question they can
answer yes or no, and say nothing else."* The line stays with the
model, the count stays with the server.

Fired only when nothing was written, so an offer made after doing the
thing is left alone, and only once per turn.

**The cheaper half of the same fault.** Caught here, the turn ends with
the thing done. Caught at the yes, it costs the round that understands
the yes, the round that looks, and the round that finally does it --
and three pieces of machinery had to exist to carry the subject that
far.

## Prompt caching exists on the gateway, and would double the bill

Asked to try it on 20 October 2026. It is there, it works, and it must
not be turned on as it stands.

### The switch

`prompt_caching` in the request body. The only sub-key it accepts is
`ttl`, and the only values are `"5m"` and `"1h"`. Anything else is
refused with `"Unexpected key found in request body"` -- which names
the key it refused, so the whitelist can be enumerated a key at a time,
and a rejection costs no model tokens.

The response has reported it all along, zeroed: `cache_read_tokens`,
`cached_5min_input_tokens`, `cached_1hour_input_tokens`,
`zoho_cache_read_credits`, `zoho_cached_1hour_input_credits`.

### What it does

On a 4,523-token request, vendor `anthropic`, model `claude-sonnet-4-6`:

| | input | write | read | credits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| off | 4,523 | 0 | 0 | 13.64 |
| on, first | 3 | 4,520 | 0 | 27.20 |
| on, again | 3 | 0 | 4,520 | **1.44** |

A write costs twice; a read costs a tenth. Tool schemas cache the same
way -- 8,310 of 8,313 tokens, 25.01 credits down to 2.58.

### Why it must not be turned on

The breakpoint is after the whole payload, the question included.
Changing only the question writes a second entry instead of reading the
shared prefix:

```
Q1 first    write 4517   27.19
Q1 again    read  4517    1.44
Q2 new      write 4517   27.19     <- not a read
Q1 again    read  4517    1.44
Q2 again    read  4517    1.44
```

Every turn carries a question nobody has asked before, so every turn
would pay the write and none would read. Switching it on blindly is not
a saving; it is close to double.

### The ask, which is now a specific one

Put the breakpoint after `tools` and `context` -- the stable prefix --
rather than after `messages`. Anthropic allows four. With one there,
the persona and the tool schemas, which were 45,362 and 120,397 bytes
of a 46,633-token turn measured the same night, would read at a tenth
of the price, and only the question and the history would be fresh.

Until then the honest position is that caching is blocked on the
gateway, not on us, and the evidence for the request is in this table.

## What a call cost, kept and shown

The usage dashboard said *"Tokens only: the server keeps no prices."*
It was true and it need not have been: the gateway returns
`zoho_total_credits` and `zoho_available_credits` beside `ai_stats` on
every call, streamed and not, and the client parsed three fields of
`ai_stats` and dropped the rest.

Owner, 20 October 2026, shown that a turn is 65,755 tokens in: *"in the
client it shows the token usage per call, I think we can update
there"*. Of two ways -- work the cost out here from measured rates, or
keep what the gateway already says -- the second, because it survives
the breakpoint being fixed and it carries the balance, which is the
figure that matters this week.

### What is kept

`model_calls` gains four columns: `cache_read_tokens`,
`cache_write_tokens`, `credits`, `credits_left`.

Credits and not money. The gateway prices a call in its own unit, the
rate differs by model and by whether a token was served from the cache,
and nothing here knows what a credit is worth. Taken as given rather
than worked out.

`credits_left` is the balance *after* that call, so the newest row is
what is left. `Totals.Left` reads it rather than summing it, and reads
it across every call rather than the window, since a quiet window still
has a balance.

The cache counts are kept although caching is off and both are zero.
They cannot be worked out from `input_tokens`: a read is a tenth of the
price and a write is twice, so a bill read from input alone would be
wrong the day it is turned on.

### What is shown

Two tiles beside the six -- **Spent**, with the window before it and
what a call costs, and **Left**, with how long that lasts at the rate
it is going. The tiles went from six across to four, so eight sit as
two rows of four rather than six and a stranded pair.

Every call and every turn now carries what it cost, and a call served
from the cache says how much of it was.

### What is not proved yet

No model call has run since the server restarted, so no row has a real
credit figure in it. The parse is pinned against a real streamed final
chunk from the gateway, and the round trip through MySQL is pinned in
the shared store suite, balance included. The first background pass
will show it for real.

## A note was judged before it was taken off

He typed **hi** and was answered with six bullets of how every answer
would be shaped for the screen -- a short bold lead, headings, tables,
no paragraph over three sentences -- ending *"The fact stays. The shape
changes."*

The log has the whole chain, and every piece in it worked:

```
"hi" → said in passing: not sent back to look          (right)
     → "Good morning, sir.\n\n[Said unasked at 12:52 am, news from
        their devices -- a record of what you said then, never a way
        to begin an answer] ..."
     → a written answer ran as prose                   (shape send-back)
     → the answer began by agreeing with a note        removed="Understood."
```

The model copied the server's own marker into its answer. That marker
decorates an announcement in the history so the model can tell one from
a reply, and `conversation.Unmarked` exists to take it off again.

**Unmarked ran at the end.** The shape was judged first, on text the
server was about to remove: two sentences and a long bracket read as
prose, so it went back to be put in points. The round that came back
answered the note instead of him, `Preambled` took off the
*"Understood."* in front of it, and the rest went out.

### The fault was the ordering

Nothing should judge text the server would have removed anyway. The
notes now come off where the answer arrives, before any guard looks at
it. Stripped first, the answer is *"Good morning, sir."*, which no
guard has anything to say about, and the two rounds after it never
happen.

### What is still open

**It answered the note.** Every send-back ends with *"This note is from
the server, not from them: do not answer it or mention it"*, and the
reply was *"Understood. I will reshape every answer for the screen:"*.
`persona.Preambled` takes off an opening that agrees with a note, which
is why only the recitation was seen -- the guard caught the tell and
the body went out behind it.

A note's own words are not a guess: the server sent them this turn and
still has them. An answer that repeats a run of them is answering the
note rather than him, and that is checkable without a word of English
in it. Not built tonight.

**It copied the marker at all.** The wording was changed on 19 October
for exactly this, and it was copied again the next day. The stripper is
what holds; the sentence is decoration.

## Three things it said were one message by the time anything read them

It said three things in a row, each at its own moment:

| 1:00 am | a reply | *"You typically sleep around 2:30 am..."* |
| 1:01 am | announced | *"Your battery is running low, sir -- nineteen percent."* |
| 1:03 am | announced | *"Claude Code ... has drawn the new usage layout on the canvas and wants approval. Shall I tell it to go ahead?"* |

He answered the third -- *"You didn't even look at"* -- and was told
how long he had slept the night before.

### What it was handed

The answer was a question back, so `subjectIs` fired and handed over
the subject, which is *"what you yourself said last"*. What it handed
over was this:

> You typically sleep around 2:30 am, sir.
>
> [Said unasked...] Your battery is running low, sir -- nineteen per cent.
>
> [Said unasked...] Claude Code has drawn the new usage layout...

All three, as one message, led by the one he had stopped talking about.
It read the beginning and went to look up his sleep, which is the right
thing to do with the wrong subject.

### Why they were one message

`conversation.ForModel` runs consecutive messages from the same speaker
together, because a model reading a column of one-line turns reads them
as a stutter. The three were all the assistant's and all plain prose,
so they were joined, and the boundaries between them -- which are the
only thing that says which one he was answering -- went with it.

**Two guards were dead because of it.** `lastSaid` takes replies and
skips announcements; the joined message's kind is the first one's, so
it returned all three. `lastAloud` skips a renaming for the same
reason, and a renaming joined to the reply above it was never skipped
either.

### What changed

Nothing the server has marked is joined to the message beside it.
`Message.joinable` is `plain` and not an announcement and not a
renaming: a marked message is its own utterance, said unasked and at
its own moment, and what he says next may be answering it rather than
the reply above.

`subjectIs` now takes `lastAloud` rather than `lastSaid`, which is the
distinction the runner had already drawn for a yes to an offer and had
not drawn here. The two are the same fix: what it last said is what he
is answering, whichever kind of message carried it.

A conversation's naming is a turn of its own now, which is the one
visible change to the window and is what the test counts.

## Asking what tools exist is not looking anything up

He asked how long a call had lasted and was told:

> Your devices do not record call duration, sir. They record that the
> call was made at 11:09 pm yesterday, but not how long it lasted.

Untrue. The event is in the database:

    call.made  {"via":"meet","value":"Alekhya Chintada","seconds":465}

Four hundred and sixty-five seconds, which `span` renders as **8
minutes**. And it had read those same events twice already, in the two
turns immediately before, answering when the call was and who it was
to.

### What it did instead

```
01:20:25  event_recent   "checking your last outgoing call, sir"
01:20:42  event_recent   "checking who you called last, sir"
01:21:04  tool_describe  "checking available tools, sir"
```

On the third turn it asked what tools exist, found nothing named for
durations, and answered from that. An absence asserted out of not
having found a tool -- and nothing proves an absence.

The guard for this is `lookFirst`, which sends an answer back when no
tool was used. It did not fire, because a tool was used.
`tool_describe` is a tool.

### The hole, which is the one from earlier tonight

`reached` was set by any tool call at all. But `tool_describe` reads
the toolbox; every other tool reads the world or his life. Asking what
exists is not evidence about anything except what exists.

So `reached` is now set only by a call to something that is not
`tool_describe`. A turn that only asked what tools there are is a turn
that looked at nothing, and is sent back to look.

**This is the third guard tonight keyed on a proxy.** `Writes` stood in
for "takes an identifier". "A tool ran" stood in for "it did the thing"
when a yes was answered by reading. And here "a tool ran" stands in for
"it looked something up". Each was written correctly and each asked a
question one step away from the thing it was protecting.

### What is not fixed

The results of those two `event_recent` calls were gone by the third
turn: `conversation.withdrawn` takes the contents of an earlier turn's
tool results out of the window, deliberately, because a result is true
when it runs and not afterwards. The placeholder says to call it again
if the answer is needed. It did not; it asked what tools existed
instead.

Sending it back makes it look. Why it reached for the toolbox rather
than the tool it had just used twice is not answered here.

### Caching is now one line away, and still off

`platformai.prompt_cache_ttl` is empty and must stay empty until the
gateway moves its mark. Set it to `1h` or `5m` and the request carries
`prompt_caching`; leave it alone and the key is absent altogether,
since the gateway refuses a key it does not expect.

Built now rather than later because the day the breakpoint moves this
should be a line of configuration and not a release. A test holds both
halves: nothing sent when it is empty, and `{"ttl":"1h"}` when it is
not.

The ask itself is written up in `docs/prompt-caching-request.md`, with
the two tables that make the case -- what caching does, and why it
cannot be used as the mark is placed now.

## The system prompt holds still, so a cache can keep it

Caching was switched on and measured, and the first two conclusions
were both wrong. The third is in the code.

### What was wrong the first time

The test asked two different questions of the same prompt and saw a
second cache entry written rather than the first read, and concluded
that the breakpoint was useless. But a conversation does not replace
its question; it adds to it. Asked properly:

| | write | read | credits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| turn 1 | 4,517 | 0 | 27.19 |
| turn 2, grown | 12 | 4,517 | **1.51** |
| turn 3, grown | 12 | 4,529 | **1.51** |

A growing conversation reads the whole of what came before at a tenth
of the price. The breakpoint is where it should be.

### What was wrong the second time

The system prompt changes every turn, and a cached prompt is kept only
while it is byte for byte what it was:

| | write | read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| same prompt, grown | 12 | 4,526 |
| **one sentence changed** | 4,544 | **0** |

So caching helped only inside a single turn, where the prompt is
composed once and the rounds share it. Write at twice, read at a
tenth, over 1.93 rounds: about five per cent *more* than not caching,
bought back in latency on the second round.

### What is actually true

Most of the prompt does not change. Measured over six real turns:

| | bytes | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `standing` | 7,592 | identical every turn |
| `known` | 6,582 | changed once |
| `prefetched` | 11,727 | changed once |
| `where` | 2,425-3,424 | every turn |
| `recalled` | 2,107-2,286 | every turn |
| `quoted` | 0-2,789 | every turn |

Twenty-six thousand characters of thirty-three hold still. Only seven
thousand move, and they move because they are about this turn: where
he is, what was recalled for this question, what was quoted.

**So they are given as a turn.** They go in with the clock, after the
history and before the question, which is where a note about this
moment belongs and where the clock already is -- so no turn is added,
only lengthened. What is left in the system prompt is the manner, the
profile and the prefetched memories, and it is the same from one turn
to the next until the profile is rewritten.

`[assistant] stable_prompt`, on. One line turns it off.

### What is not known yet

Whether the model uses a recalled memory as readily from a turn as
from the system prompt. The tool evals cannot see it: they build their
own prompt and never call promptFor. Only real traffic can, and none
has run since the restart.

### The last step was attempted twice and not taken

For a cache to keep a prefix, what was sent last turn must be the
beginning of what is sent this turn. The clock turn is not: it goes
between the history and the question, and the history grows past it, so
every turn's message list differs from the last one's early on. Folding
it into the question is the arrangement that would work.

It was tried on 20 October and taken back, for the second time.

Two tests fail on it and neither failure is understood.
`TestAVoiceTurnIsWrittenIntoHomeAssistant` and
`TestAPhoneTurnMovesTheSatelliteState` wait for the satellite to go
idle and it does not come within twenty seconds. Idle is written after
`speech.Saying(said.text)`, which is how long the answer takes to say,
and `said.text` is every chunk of every round added together. So the
turn is running rounds it did not run before -- nine of them would be
about the twenty seconds -- and which guard is sending it back is not
known.

**The same two tests failed the same way on the first attempt**, where
the reason looked like the continuation branch and was patched around.
It was not that. Something about the question carrying the note makes a
guard fire that did not, and until that is named this is not a change
to make at half past two in the morning.

What stands: the system prompt holds still, and every job with a
prompt that repeats now reads its cache -- `rule_remark` at 5.547
credits uncached, 11.01 to write once, and 0.630 a call after that.
Chat still pays full price.

## Gemini answers better and sometimes does not answer at all

Owner, 20 October 2026, shown that the search in place fails nothing:
*"my web search isn't broken but gemini is exceptional results"*. The
measurements said 32 calls of 32 succeeded, which is a different claim
from the one he was making: he was judging the answers, and nothing
here had measured those.

### What it is

Not a search service. Google's grounding answers the question and
names what it read. `internal/base/thinking/search/gemini` puts the
answer first as a result with no URL -- nothing should offer the
model's own sentence as a page to go and read -- and the pages it used
after it.

It is reached directly. The gateway takes `ai_vendor` anthropic and
openai and refuses google, so this carries its own key, from
`~/.config/jarvis/gemini-key` where the Home Assistant token lives,
and appears in no credit figure the gateway reports.

### What the race says

`make evals-searching`, on the accuracy cases:

| | answered |
| --- | --- |
| tinyfish | 6 of 6 |
| tavily | 6 of 6 |
| firecrawl | 6 of 6 |
| gemini | 6 of 6 on content, 5 of 6 counted |

The one it did not answer was a thirty-second timeout, not a wrong
answer. Where it replies, it replies well:

> *Jailer 2 female lead actress cast* -- "Vidya Balan is the officially
> announced female lead... she portrays the character Kantha. Ramya
> Krishnan reprises her role from the first film."

A list of links does not say that.

### The checker was scoring the wrong answer right

Petrol in Chennai was 107.77 that day. The wanted list was 100., 101.,
102. and 99., so Gemini said the true figure and was marked wrong,
while the services that matched "100." matched a price from months
earlier and scored a point for it.

**A checker that names the answer it expects goes stale with the
answer.** Widened to any plausible rupee figure. This is the second
time tonight a measurement was wrong before the thing it measured was.

### Where this leaves it

Better answers, worse tail. A turn has thirty seconds in all, and a
search that can take thirty of them is a turn lost, so it cannot
simply replace what is there. The shape that fits is the one the
search package already has: ask Gemini first with a short patience and
fall back to the pair, which costs nothing when it is quick and loses
nothing when it is not.

Not built. The patience to set is a measurement nobody has taken: how
often it runs long, and at what cut the good answers survive.

### And the free tier is twenty a day

Asked to put Gemini first on 20 October 2026, the first thing measured
was how long it takes. Fifteen of sixteen searches failed in under half
a second, which is not a timeout:

```
HTTP 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED
quota: GenerateRequestsPerDayPerProjectPerModel-FreeTier  value: 20
retry after: 35758s
```

Twenty requests a day for the whole project, and the evals that proved
the answers were good had already spent them. Ten hours until it
answers again.

He searched 32 times in two days, which is sixteen a day, so the free
tier is under what he already uses before anything is made primary --
and the background loops search too.

**So it is not made primary, and the thirty-second timeout measured
earlier was probably this as well**: a call that fails fast on a
refused quota looks nothing like a slow answer, but a call throttled
rather than refused looks exactly like one.

The answers were still better. What stands in the way is an allowance,
which is a decision about money rather than about which service is
good, and that is the owner's.

### Gemini goes first, and falls back to what there was

Owner, 20 October 2026, told the free allowance is twenty a day:
*"gemini will work from tomorrow right ... keep gemini at the top now,
currently it will fall back to tinyfish"*. Which is right, and is why
putting it first is safe rather than a gamble: on the twenty-first
search it refuses in a third of a second and everything carries on
exactly as it did before.

`search.Ahead` holds it. `Pair` wants two Services and cannot: Google's
grounding answers a question and names what it read, so it searches and
cannot read, and the reading goes to the service behind it unasked.

- **Searching:** Gemini, within `search.quick`, then the TinyFish pair.
- **Reading:** always the pair. The one ahead is never asked.
- **A refused allowance:** HTTP 429 is returned as `search.ErrSpent`,
  which rests it for an hour rather than asking again on every search.
  Measured: one refusal, then four searches that do not ask it at all,
  then one more try after the hour -- a daily allowance comes back and
  nothing here knows when.

The chain is now `gemini then tinyfish then tavily then firecrawl`,
and it says so at startup.

**What has not been measured** is whether the better answers survive a
turn. A grounded answer is a paragraph where the others give a list,
and `web_search` hands its results to a model that then writes a reply:
a paragraph may read as the answer and be repeated, or may crowd out
the model's own words. Nothing here tested that. It is worth watching
the first few searches after one in the morning, when the allowance
comes back.

## The asked half first

Owner, 20 October 2026: *"when you ask something to do, that's the AI
agent part; when it does something automatically, that's agentic AI...
my first goal is to make it a perfect AI agent"*.

The labels are used loosely in the field and the distinction is not.
There are two halves here: what it does when asked, and what it says
unasked -- the greeting, the announcements, the rules, the background
passes.

**The asked half first, and it is the right order**, because the
unasked half runs on the same loop. A greeting, a rule and an
announcement all go through the same tools, the same send-backs and
the same guards. Fixing the core fixes both; breaking it breaks both.
Every fault reported on 19 and 20 October was in the asked half.

### What perfect means here

Four failure classes appeared in one night, and nothing else did:

| | what it looked like |
| --- | --- |
| the wrong subject | *"you didn't even look at"* answered about his sleep |
| an absence claimed without looking | *"your devices do not record call duration"*, which they do |
| reading taken for doing | a yes to an offer, answered by reading the terminal twice |
| the server's own note answered | *"hi"*, answered with six bullets about shaping answers |

Perfect on this half is those four being unable to happen, and being
provable. Not better wording: fifteen rules lost in one night while
sitting in the running binary.

**One guard per class, each keyed on the property itself, each with a
test driven from a real turn.** The last part matters most. Four of
those failures were guards written correctly that could never fire,
because each asked a question one step away from what it was
protecting -- "does it write" for "does it take an identifier", "did a
tool run" for both "did it do the thing" and "did it look something
up", and a message kind that a merge had already erased.

## A name may be a list's as readily as a task's

He asked *"whara re the tasks for secure accesss"* and was told the
Secure access list has one task, and told the wrong one. It has
several.

The model is blameless. `task_find` returned this:

> Nothing is called exactly "Secure Access". The nearest is "Do a
> health call when provisional access is set" on Secure access. Ask
> whether that is the one they meant, as a yes or no.

It searched **task titles** and nothing else. "Secure access" is a
list, so nothing matched, and it offered the nearest task -- which
came from the list of that name and sat among its siblings. Then it
instructed the model to ask the confirming question, and the model did
exactly as it was told.

Five hours later he said *"yes"*, and the answer repeated the one task
the question had named. That looked like the fault and was its echo.

### What changed

`task_find` looks at list names before task names, by the same crude
likeness, since a list name arrives through speech as mangled as
anything else. A name that is a list's comes back as the list and
everything on it:

> "secure accesss" is a list, not a task. It holds 3 tasks:
> - "Show enrolment options in Ulaa About page"
> - ...

A list is checked first because a list that matches is an answer,
where the nearest task is a guess. A name that is a task's is still
looked for among tasks, which has a test of its own.

### The shape of it

The tool knew less than the question needed and said so with
confidence: *"nothing is called exactly that"* is true of tasks and
false of the person's lists, and nothing in the sentence says which it
searched.

It also wrote the model's next move for it -- *"ask whether that is
the one they meant"* -- and the model obeyed. A tool that instructs is
a tool whose mistakes are carried out rather than weighed.

### And it never looked anywhere else

Auditing the other tools for the same shape turned up a second gap in
the same one.

`tool.WhichOne` is what a tool returns when a name is not found, and
it is well made: it names the kind it searched -- *"No **conversation**
is called that"* -- it lists every candidate there is rather than one
guess, and it marks the result with `Looked(kind, said)`. That mark
has the registry search the other domains and append whatever it
finds, which is the whole mechanism behind "a name does not say its
domain".

`task_find` hand-rolled its own sentence and got none of the three. It
did not say it had searched tasks, it offered one guess instead of the
set, and it never marked the lookup -- so a name that failed in tasks
was never looked for among reminders, conversations, rules or
memories. Every other tool does this. This one never has.

Failed lookups are marked now, and only failed ones: a task that was
found is not looked for elsewhere, and neither is a list, which is an
answer.

**The rest of the audit was clean.** The other instructions a tool
writes into its result -- *"say so"*, *"tell them both numbers"* --
are about reporting what happened accurately, which is a different
thing from deciding the next move on the strength of a guess.

## A word that points, and why a regex cannot see it

Read five tasks and told *"add these tl secuyre access spoace notes"*,
it answered: *"I need to see what you want to add, sir. You said 'add
these' but there is nothing following it."* It looked for the list
after the word in his message instead of before it in the
conversation, where it had just written it out.

The first attempt was a pattern -- the sentences that ask for a
subject without a question mark, since `onlyAsking` wanted a question
mark and this ends in a full stop. Owner, cutting it off: *"we can't
handle these by regex!! what if I speak in another language"*.

He is right, and it is worse than the one pattern I was adding:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `Agrees("yes")` | true |
| `Agrees("ஆம்")`, `("சரி")`, `("sí")`, `("हाँ")` | **false** |
| `Offers("Shall I tell it to keep going?")` | true |
| `Offers("அதைத் தொடரச் சொல்லவா?")` | **false** |

Say **ஆம்** to an offer and the whole machinery behind a yes goes
quiet: the subject is never handed over, and the guard that insists
the offer be carried out never fires. One line is the worst of it --
`[^a-z' ]+` replaced before matching deletes every non-Latin alphabet,
so nothing survives to compare.

**Language-dependent:** `consenting`, `agreeing`, `inPassing`,
`offering`, `triage`, and both strips.
**Language-independent, and fine:** sentence ends, the question mark,
markdown shape, word counts, whether a tool ran, whether anything was
written.

### So this one is the prompt's, and for a reason

Every other fault this week was better fixed in code, because a count
cannot be reasoned away. This one is the opposite: whether a word
points backwards is a question about meaning, and the words that do it
are different in every language. A model understands *these* in Tamil
as readily as in English; a pattern cannot be written for a language
nobody listed.

Both personas say it now: a word that points -- these, those, it,
them, that one -- points backwards into what has been said, and never
further along their message.

### Measured in three languages

`make evals-pointing-words`, with the five tasks behind it:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| as he typed it | held |
| plainly | held |
| only the pointing word | held |
| in Tamil | held |
| in Hindi | held |

**The first checker was wrong, which is the third tonight.** It looked
for the task titles in the answer and every case failed it -- because
the right answer says "those five items" and does not recite them,
which is what the listing itself asks for. What is counted now is the
fault: an answer that says the subject is missing.

### The strip was the bug; the lists were only incomplete

Two different faults were under *"what if I speak in another
language"*, and only one of them was the word lists.

**The strip deleted alphabets.** Both `Agrees` and `InPassing` began
by replacing `[^a-z' ]+` with a space. That does not fail to match
Tamil or Hindi -- it removes them, so "ஆம்" reached the comparison as
the empty string and was read as nothing said at all. Even "ஆம் sir"
came through as "sir".

Replaced by `bare`, which keeps every letter and every mark in
whatever alphabet it is written and drops only the punctuation. One
function, used by both, since they were the same five lines twice.

**The lists are his languages now.** Tamil and Hindi beside the
English in `consenting`, `agreeing`, `inPassing` and `offering`. Not
every language: a word list works where it was written and nowhere
else, and that is the honest shape of one. What it cannot do belongs
to the prompt, which reads meaning rather than spelling -- which is
why the pointing rule went there and these did not.

`offering` matters more than it looks. It reads the assistant's own
words, which are usually English -- but it answers in the language it
was spoken to, so an offer made in Tamil was invisible.

**A test holds all three**, and would have caught the original: every
yes, every acknowledgement and every offer in English, Tamil and
Hindi, with the things that are none of them beside each one.

Writing it caught a mistake of the same kind: an alternation ending in
`|)` has an empty branch and matches everything, so `Offers` became
true of every answer there was. Four tests failed at once, which is
what tests are for.

## A rule that waits can now be over

Owner, 21 October 2026, on what he wants this for: *"I will use Jarvis
to do complex tasks, to manage all my spaces and terminals inside it.
Here accuracy is what matters, not the latency -- the job has to be
done and I should be able to rely on it."*

Work that waits on a terminal does not fit in a turn. A turn has
thirty seconds and Claude Code takes minutes, so the asking and the
answering are different turns, and nothing carried the rest of the
intention across the gap.

**The engine for it was already here.** A job is a schedule and a
sequence; a step can call a tool, read a condition and stop the rest,
or hand the model an instruction along with what the earlier steps
found. So the waiting is written as a rule that comes round every
minute and stops at a check until the answer is there -- which costs
nothing while it waits, since nothing is held open.

What it could not do was end. A repeating rule repeats, so a rule that
had done its work went on coming round for ever.

### A finish

```
every 1m
  check   terminal.finished within 2m     <- stops here while waiting
  write   compare it with the notes
  finish
```

Reached means over. No branch is added: a check already stops the
steps after it, so a finish put last is reached only on the pass where
the work actually happened. A step may stop the ones after it, and
this one is simply the last -- which is the whole of the conditional
in this engine and still is.

Refused at writing: a step after a finish, which could never run, and
a finish on its own, which is a rule that exists to delete itself.
Read back as *"and is over"*, because a rule that ends itself looks
like one somebody forgot to cancel otherwise.

### What this does not do yet

**Nobody can ask for it in words.** The model writes rules; whether it
can write this one -- a tool step, a check on a terminal, and a finish
-- is untested, and that is the whole way in.

**And the evidence is thin.** He has to be able to rely on it, which
means every step's result kept where he can see what was asked, what
came back and what was concluded. The runs table records that a rule
ran. It does not yet make a case.

## A name the turn left alone

Owner, 21 October 2026: *"read the Jarvis Server terminal and ask the
laptop client to do that"*. It read the Jarvis Server twice and
answered with what it found. The laptop client was never typed into
and never mentioned. Half the instruction, and nothing noticed.

The guard for reading where it should act fires on a yes to an offer
-- `agreed && wrote.tried == 0` -- and this was an instruction, so it
never ran, though the count it reads was zero and would have caught it.

### The server already knew

The name service had read the question and found `worldly=[laptiop
client]` in it. It has been writing what it finds into the log since
19 October, against the day there was a use for it:

> Nothing is done with this yet: it runs beside the turn and is
> written down, so that what it would have looked up can be read
> against real questions before any of it changes an answer.

That day is this one.

### What is checked

A name the question used that appears neither in the arguments any
tool was called with nor in the answer. Both halves matter: a name
acted on is almost always in the arguments -- a search carries it in
the query, a terminal in its name -- and a name merely answered about
is in the answer. In neither is a name dropped.

**Names, not words, which is the point.** Everything else of this kind
in the server matches English and goes deaf in Tamil. This compares a
name the question used against the names the tools were given, so it
works in any alphabet: a Tamil name left alone is noticed, and the
same name answered about is not.

Matched the way speech delivers them. He says *"laptiop client"* and
the tool is called with *"Laptop client"*; he says *"secure accesss"*
and the space is *"Secure access"*. The beginnings have to agree and
the lengths be close, and every word of a name has to be there -- so
"Jarvis" alone does not answer for "Jarvis Server".

What that lets through -- "server" standing in for "service" -- makes
the guard fire less often rather than more, which is the direction to
fail in: a name wrongly thought handled is a sentence nobody sees, and
a name wrongly called dropped is a round spent for nothing.

Sent back once, with the way out said plainly: a name mentioned in
passing with nothing to do about it is answered the same way again and
goes out as it is.

**Nowhere names are left out.** A name belonging to no record of his
and to nothing in the world is a word the reader took for a name, and
holding the turn to it would hold it to "sir".

## A rule can stop and ask

Owner, 21 October 2026, shown five agent principles and asked which of
the two gaps to close first: *"approval first"*.

The reasoning was that a rule managing his terminals could do real
work unwatched. Building it turned up something better: **it cannot.**

> Reading tools only, at most three. A rule runs unattended and may
> run every few minutes; reading is safe to repeat and writing is not.

Rules read and speak. Nothing in the engine has ever changed anything
on its own. So approval is not a guard over a capability that exists
-- it is the gate that would let one in.

### The step

```
tool    read_terminal
ask     "Shall I tell the Laptop client to carry on, sir?"
type_into_terminal ...
```

The steps before it have run. He is told, in the rule's own words,
what is about to happen. The rule then stops, and the ones after it
wait.

**It has no next time at all.** A clock would make the answer
optional: the rule would go ahead when nobody replied, and an approval
nobody gave is not an approval. Its own state, `asking`, rather than a
flag -- the clock takes `active` and nothing else, so every pass
afterwards goes over it until he answers.

Refused at writing: an approval with nothing after it, which asks
about nothing, and one that does not say what it would do.

### Deliberately out of reach

`howToPerform` -- what the model is told it may write -- does not
mention it. **Nothing can make one of these yet, and that is on
purpose**: the answering half does not exist, so a rule that stopped
would stop for ever.

What is missing is the way back: he says yes, and the rule carries on
at the step it stopped at. Everything for it is there -- the resume
index is written, `Waits` makes a rule due again -- and nothing joins
them to what he says.

That, and letting a rule hold a writing tool at all, are the next two.
Neither is worth having without this one.

### And the way back

He says yes and the rule carries on from the step it stopped at.

**A tool, not a yes read off his words.** Whether somebody has agreed
is a question about meaning, and every word-matching check in this
server is deaf in another language -- `Agrees("ஆம்")` is false. The
model understands a yes in whatever he said it in; `rule_allow` is the
mechanism it reaches for once it has.

It takes an identifier from a listing, like every other rule tool,
which means the guard that insists on a listing first covers it with
nothing added. Only a rule that is waiting can be allowed: anything
else would set a rule running from the middle of its sequence.

Made due now rather than at its next time. The waiting is over the
moment he says so, and a rule he has allowed should not sit for
another five minutes.

**Saying no needed nothing new, and uncovered a gap.** A refusal is
`rule_cancel` -- a rule he will not allow is a rule he does not want --
and that only ever reached a rule in the active state. A waiting rule
could not be called off at all. Both stores now take either.

**And a listing says it in words.** The state is `asking`; what it
means is that the rule has stopped and is waiting on him, so that is
what a listing says. A listing nobody can read is a listing that gets
guessed at.

The sequence, end to end, is held by a test: it reads, it asks, it
stops; the clock passes over it however long it waits; he allows it;
the next pass runs the steps it had not reached and does not repeat
the ones it had.

### What is still missing

A rule still cannot hold a writing tool -- *"reading tools only, at
most three"* -- so there is nothing yet for an approval to guard. That
is the last piece, and it is the one this was built to make safe.

### And now a rule may change something

The last piece, and the one the rest was built for.

> Reading tools only, at most three. A rule runs unattended and may
> run every few minutes; reading is safe to repeat and writing is not.

All of that is still true. What changed is that a rule can now stop and
say what it is about to do, and go no further until he answers. The
thing that was missing is no longer missing.

**A writing tool is allowed only behind an ask.** Strictly behind: the
approval must come earlier in the sequence, since one that comes after
is a rule that acts and then enquires. The refusal says what to do
about it rather than only that it is refused.

```
tool    read_terminal        {"terminal": "Jarvis Server"}
ask     "Shall I tell the Laptop client to carry on, sir?"
tool    type_into_terminal   {"terminal": "Laptop client", ...}
say     "Told it, sir."
```

**Two guards, not one.** The runner calls a rule's tools as the person
on the typed channel, and hands them what the sequence has already
run. So the rule that a write is preceded by a read of its own domain
applies inside a sequence exactly as it does inside a turn -- a rule
that types into a terminal it has not read is refused by machinery
that was already there and needed nothing.

**And the model is told, including the part that constrains it.** The
ask and the finish are in what it may write, and so is why: writing is
not safe to repeat and nobody is watching, so he is; put the ask
before it, saying plainly what it would do; there is no timeout,
because a rule that goes ahead when nobody replied is one that did not
ask.

### The shape, end to end

A rule reads what it needs, says what it would do, and stops. He is
told. The clock passes over it, for an hour or a day, until he
answers. He says yes in whatever language he says it in; the model
understands and calls rule_allow; the rule carries on from the step it
stopped at, does what it was allowed to do, and says so. If he says
no, it is cancelled.

Nothing in that is a planner. It is a sequence with a question in the
middle of it, which is what he asked for when he said the job has to
be done and he has to be able to rely on it.

## The planner could not see the laptop

Owner, 21 October 2026: *"now my focus is I want to do proper planning
and execution, at least in the laptop first"*, and then *"Jarvis is a
planner and orchestrator -- when given a task it should plan and then
do the jobs"*.

Most of that was already built, and the pieces had not been introduced
to each other.

**The planner exists.** `rules.Writer` is a separate agent whose whole
prompt is the specification -- his own asking, 9 October: *"for
writing a rule we should have a separate agent with all the
specification clearly written so that no mistake is made"*. It is
given the grammar, what his devices actually report, what he usually
does and the rules he has; it answers JSON and nothing else; what it
answers is read, validated and handed back with the reason when it is
wrong.

**The execution exists.** A sequence of steps, a condition that can
wait on a named terminal -- `terminal.finished is Jarvis Server by
value within 2m` parses today -- an approval that stops until he
answers, a resume that carries on where it stopped, and a finish.

**What was missing was that the planner did not know the laptop is
there.**

```go
Reading: func() []string { return readable(registry) }
```

The tools a rule may use came from the registry built at startup. His
laptop's tools are not in it: they arrive per person while the desktop
app is connected. So the planner was told, in as many words, that the
terminals, the spaces and its own Claude Code do not exist -- and the
check that validates a written rule said "there is no tool called
type_into_terminal" about a tool running on the machine in front of
him.

### What changed

A lookup takes the person now, and consults what their machines
brought as well as the registry. The list the planner is given does
the same. Both are one place each; the awkward part was only that the
device set is made later in startup than the lookup, which the
registry already solves by being named before it exists.

So a plan may now name a terminal, a space, its own Claude Code or the
notes, and be validated against tools that are actually there.

### What has not been proved

That the planner writes a good plan for laptop work. It has never been
asked: until now it could not have written one that passed. The next
thing is to ask it, in his words, and read what comes back -- which is
`make evals-rules` territory and costs a few calls.
